payload.title: fix(update): unrelated transitional Windows services no longer abort updates (salvage of #96381)

payload.author: VibeSan7
payload.body:
Independent Windows 11 confirmation for the `START_PENDING` variant:

- The current pre-fix implementation reproduced with the unrelated Windows `DiagTrack` service reporting `status=start_pending` and a live PID.
- The Desktop handoff failed with `SCM service DiagTrack has indeterminate status: start_pending` -> `SCM service enumeration failed` -> exit 1.
- With an equivalent ancestry-scoped local patch, `find_windows_gateway_services()` completed without raising while `DiagTrack` remained `start_pending`.
- Two real Desktop `Update now` cycles then completed with exit 0 (`ac6c8028` -> `2c232761` -> `e387cbc0`), including Gateway stop/restart and Desktop rebuild.
- Focused local validation across all tests that reference this function: **69 passed, 5 skipped**; Ruff passed. Telegram polling and the Gateway were healthy again after restart.

This is direct field evidence that the semantics in #97929 fix `START_PENDING`, not only the `STOP_PENDING` case used by its success-path regression test. A small follow-up improvement would be to parameterize that test with `start_pending` as well, since it pins the exact state observed here (and in #97856).

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed PR #97900 (`fix(desktop): preserve batch clarify choices after skip`).

The fix surfaces the original `choices_offered` on skipped batch rows so the user can still pick a late answer after the batch was skipped, and falls back to the args-declared questions/choices when the response row omits them. The `useMemo` around `readClarifyArgs` and the `row.choices === undefined ? fallback : row.choices` precedence are both sensible.

Non-blocking observations:

- **Index alignment between `responses` and `fallbackQuestions`.** The fallback lookup is positional (`fallbackQuestions?.[index]`). If the settled batch response ever reorders, drops, or dedupes rows relative to the args order, the fallback question/choices would silently attach to the wrong row. The args order and response order appear to match today (and the new tests cover the aligned case), so this is defensive: consider keying by `id` when present instead of position if a mismatch is possible.
- **Empty-choices edge case.** When `choices_offered` is present but empty, `readClarifyBatchResult` stores `null` and the row renders no late choices even though the fallback args may still have choices. That's a deliberate "authoritative empty" signal, but it's worth being aware that a provider returning `choices_offered: []` will suppress the fallback choices entirely. If that's unintended, treating `[]` as "unknown" (falling back) rather than "no choices" would be safer.

No blocking issues; the new tests (skipped row keeps actionable choices; answered row renders none) directly cover the regression.

payload.author: frahlg
payload.title: feat(discord): add DISCORD_DISABLE_DMS for public community bots

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed PR #97895 (`feat(discord): add DISCORD_DISABLE_DMS for public community bots`).

The feature is well-scoped: gate the `dm_messages` intent at connect, drop DMs in the message admission and `_handle_message` paths, reject slash commands in DMs with a user-facing ephemeral reply, and wire up env/config + docs + tests. Defense in depth across intent and admission is reasonable (the intent alone would not cover interaction events, which arrive regardless of message intents, so the explicit slash-command check is necessary).

Non-blocking observations:

- **Two divergent "is a DM" definitions.** `_discord_message_is_dm` treats a message as DM when the channel is a `DMChannel` *or* `guild is None` (which also catches `GroupChannel`), but `_evaluate_slash_authorization` only checks `isinstance(chan_obj, discord.DMChannel)`. A group DM slash command would therefore not be rejected when DMs are disabled, while group DM *messages* would be. Consider reusing a single helper (e.g. a channel-based `_is_dm_channel` that also handles `GroupChannel`) for both call sites so the two paths stay consistent.
- **`raw.strip().lower() in {"true","1","yes","on"}`** — the string truthiness list differs slightly from other Discord gates in the codebase (some accept `"y"`). Harmless, but worth confirming the accepted values match the docs table wording.
- Minor: `getattr(discord, "DMChannel", None)` is defensive to a fault — `discord.DMChannel` always exists in the installed library; the fallback branch is dead code in practice. Fine either way.

No blocking issues; tests cover the DM-drop and guild-mention-preserved paths.

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed PR #97893 (`fix(desktop): position find bar below titlebar to not overlap window controls`).

The change restores the real `--titlebar-height` on the find bar's own style so it clears the titlebar band, overriding the `0px` value injected by the ContribController subtree. Scoping the override to the bar element itself is clean and avoids leaking the fix.

Non-blocking observations:

- **Verify the CSS consumer reads the variable.** The diff sets `--titlebar-height` on the bar, but the consuming rule (the one that computes `top: calc(var(--titlebar-height) + 0.5rem)` or similar) is outside this diff. If any rule hardcodes `top: 0.5rem` or reads a different variable, the override silently does nothing. Worth a quick check that the find-bar styles actually consume this var (this looks like it's the case per the linked issue, but it's not visible in this change).
- **Minor:** `...(filesPaneRight != null ? { right: ... } : {})` — the empty-object branch is unnecessary since spreading `{}` is a no-op; `filesPaneRight != null ? { right: ... } : undefined` would read slightly cleaner, but this is purely stylistic.

No blocking issues.

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed PR #97892 (`fix(desktop): clear stale macOS backend ownership records`).

The change centralizes the process-probe "missing process" decision in `processProbeConfirmsMissing` and adds the Darwin-only interpretation of a numeric exit code `1` from `ps -p <pid>` (Node surfaces it as a numeric `error.code` rather than `ESRCH`). The platform gating is the right call, and the test table covering darwin/linux × numeric/string codes is good coverage.

Non-blocking observations:

- **`code === '1'` string form is untested but harmless.** The test only exercises `code: 1` (number) on darwin; the string `'1'` branch is covered implicitly by the `code: '1'` assertion on line 21 — actually that line covers it. Good.

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

**fix(desktop): make HUD a solid themed card, not a see-through overlay**

Substantial, well-documented CSS rework. Converting the HUD sheet from a translucent dark scrim (`rgb(12 14 18 / 0.62)`) to opaque theme paper (`var(--ui-bg-elevated)`), making the card fill the window below the bar (flush, `border-radius: 0`), and re-scoping the forced white overlay ink to `[data-hud-game]` only — while preserving the translucent scrim *over games* — directly addresses the washed-out unfocused HUD text caused by the 62% scrim + macOS vibrancy. The inline comments explaining each specificity decision are unusually good.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **`styles-contract.test.ts` reads the CSS source file.** The new test parses `src/styles.css` text (regex over selectors/declaration blocks) and asserts literal declaration values. This is effective as a *contract* test (it pins the behavior-relevant invariants: opaque paper at rest, scrim over games, no `--hud-band-height` hole), and CSS is data rather than executable code — but it is tightly coupled to CSS formatting (one-line vs multi-line, declaration order, `!important` placement) and will fail on innocuous reformats. Note the project's "never read source code in tests" guidance; if that policy extends to CSS, this test sits in a gray zone. Consider whether a lighter assertion (e.g., a couple of key selectors via an injected stylesheet snapshot or a dedicated CSS-variable token check) could keep the invariant coverage with less coupling.

2. **`var(--ui-bg-elevated)` availability.** The card now relies on `--ui-bg-elevated` being defined in the HUD window's theme scope. The contract test only asserts the *declaration* text equals the variable — it won't catch the variable being undefined/unset at runtime (which would fall back to `transparent`, recreating a see-through sheet). Worth a quick runtime check across themes.

3. **CSS-only change, no component test.** All logic here is in styles.css; the TS changes are comment-only. The contract test is the sole guard — fine given the surface, but the formatting-coupling point above is the main risk to that guard's long-term stability.

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

**fix(desktop): recover visible sessions after stale runtime RPC**

Well-scoped and carefully tested. The design is right: on a structured stale-runtime failure (code 4001) for an RPC on the *currently visible* session, request a durable rebind (`requestSessionResume`) but always rethrow the original error (preserving the error contract — it deliberately does not retry a potentially destructive RPC). The exclusions for `session.resume`/`session.activate` (the resume lifecycle itself) and for background rows (via `routingSessionId === selectedStoredSessionIdRef.current`) prevent both double-resumes and foreground route theft. The four new tests cover all the meaningful branches.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **Message-regex fallback can false-positive.** `isStaleRuntimeSessionError` falls back to `/session not found/i` only when there's no numeric code — a reasonable guard for older bridges that lose the code. But any non-coded error whose message happens to mention "session not found" (e.g., a tool output echoed into an error) would be treated as stale-runtime. Impact is limited (only the visible session, only non-resume methods, and the result is a soft `requestSessionResume`), so low risk — flagging for awareness.

2. **Recovery is fire-and-forget.** `requestSessionResume(...)` is not awaited and its failure is not surfaced to the user. If the durable resume also fails, the user sees only the original RPC error with no hint that recovery was attempted and failed. Consider logging the resume outcome (success/failure) for diagnosability.

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

**fix(cli): suppress duplicate response panel when TTS displays without token streaming**

Reasonable fix. The new per-turn `self._tts_displayed_this_turn` flag records that the TTS display callback actually rendered text, and `run_agent` now suppresses the final Rich Panel when TTS was the sole display path (the `tts_already_displayed` condition adds `self._tts_displayed_this_turn or` to the existing `_streaming_box_opened` check). 1. **Cross-thread flag.** The flag is written from the TTS consumer thread (`display_callback`) and read from the main thread in `run_agent`. For a single bool under the GIL this is fine and the comment calls it thread-safe — but if this ever needs to carry more than a boolean (e.g., a count or a last-display timestamp), switch to a lock or an atomic.

2. **Reset ordering vs. a draining previous turn.** The flag is reset to `False` at the start of `_stage_user_message`. If the *previous* turn's TTS consumer can still be draining (thread not yet joined/stopped) at that moment, a late `display_callback` from the old turn could set the flag `True` after the reset, spuriously suppressing the new turn's response panel. Confirm the TTS thread is joined/stopped before the next `_stage_user_message` runs.

payload.author: toyama2026
payload.title: fix: proxy platform webhooks past the dashboard OAuth gate

payload.author: andrexibiza
payload.body:
This is a real production failure, and the live `302 -> /auth/login` reproduction is useful evidence. The narrow path table is also the right instinct: refusing to guess routes for SMS/WhatsApp/etc. is much safer than turning a routing repair into an ambient catch-all. I checked the exact head `a837c3cad8f1107b5dd7cd26f863357ed486385d`, the full two-file diff, the current LINE/Feishu/WeCom callback implementations, middleware ordering, current-main ancestry, hosted checks, existing PR comments/reviews, and the open `web_server.py` decomposition graph.

I do not think this head is merge-ready yet. There are three correctness/security blockers plus one architecture/release gate.

### P1 — the proxy removes the adapters' pre-auth body-size boundary

`hermes_cli/web_server.py::_proxy_platform_webhook()` does:

```py
body = await request.body()
```

before the request reaches the adapter. There is no outer size cap or bounded stream read.

That is a semantic regression at the new public ingress boundary. The three adapters deliberately reject oversized *unauthenticated* bodies before doing expensive/authenticated work:

- LINE: `WEBHOOK_BODY_MAX_BYTES = 1_048_576`, enforced by `web.Application(client_max_size=WEBHOOK_BODY_MAX_BYTES)`.
- Feishu: `_FEISHU_WEBHOOK_MAX_BODY_BYTES = 1 * 1024 * 1024`, with both a bounded reader and `client_max_size` backstop.
- WeCom callback: `_MAX_BODY = 65_536`; its source explicitly says `client_max_size` must reject before the handler/signature work.

With this proxy in front, an unauthenticated Internet client can make the dashboard process buffer an arbitrarily large body *before* any of those controls can reject it. The downstream adapter cap no longer protects the process that now owns public ingress.

**Required fix:** make the proxy's read bounded by the selected platform's authoritative pre-auth body limit (do not trust `Content-Length` alone; chunked/misreported bodies still need a streaming bound), return `413` before opening the loopback request, and add regressions for all three platforms proving an oversized request never reaches `httpx.AsyncClient.request`.

### P1 — Feishu's source identity collapses to `127.0.0.1`, turning its per-peer rate limit into one attacker-drainable global bucket

Feishu's `_handle_webhook_request()` intentionally derives:

```py
remote_ip = request.remote or "unknown"
rate_key = f"{self._app_id}:{self._webhook_path}:{remote_ip}"
```

and performs that rate-limit check before verification-token/auth processing. The proxy opens a fresh loopback HTTP connection, so every Internet sender arrives at the adapter as `request.remote == 127.0.0.1`.

That means one unauthenticated sender can consume the shared 120/minute bucket and cause legitimate Feishu deliveries from every real peer to receive `429` until the window clears. This is exactly the other side of a reverse-proxy change: payload and signature survive, but transport provenance does not.

**Required fix:** preserve client provenance through a *trusted* proxy contract, not by trusting caller-supplied forwarding headers. For example: strip inbound `Forwarded`/`X-Forwarded-*`, inject a proxy-owned original-peer value, and have the Feishu adapter honor it only when its direct peer is loopback/the trusted local proxy. Add a regression where two distinct public peers remain distinct rate-limit keys, plus a spoofed inbound forwarding header that cannot choose the effective peer identity.

### P1 — `_PORT_BINDING_PLATFORM_PORTS` is display data, not the adapter's listener authority

The new resolver says it finds the adapter's "actual live port" by reusing `_PORT_BINDING_PLATFORM_PORTS` and `_profile_platform_ports()`. Current source says the opposite: that table is explicitly **"Used only for the dashboard's gateway-topology readout — best-effort display data, not a bind source"**, and the existing topology helper explicitly does not resolve env-var port overrides.

That distinction matters here:

- LINE's real li

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

**fix(desktop): surface Tailscale SSH browser checks**

Good, security-conscious change. Detecting the Tailscale "additional check" stderr and mapping it to a new `INTERACTIVE_AUTH` error kind, then emitting non-interactive guidance (`ssh <host> true`, complete the browser check, retry) is the right UX. The one-time URL is deliberately kept out of the surfaced message (the test asserts `doesNotMatch` against `login.tailscale.com`), and `stderrKind` carries only the classification through the timeout path — properly defensive about leaking a one-time auth URL through Desktop errors or lifecycle logs.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **Classification is only consulted on the timeout path.** The `stderrKind` → `INTERACTIVE_AUTH` mapping is applied inside the `if (stderrOrErr.kind === SSH_ERROR.TIMEOUT)` branch. If `ssh` exits *quickly* (non-zero, e.g. code 255) carrying the same Tailscale "additional check" stderr rather than hanging until the timeout, the guidance won't surface. Consider classifying the immediate-exit path too, or adding a test for a fast exit with that stderr.

2. **Regex requires the https scheme and exact host.** `/To authenticate, visit:\s*https:\/\/login\.tailscale\.com\//` won't match if Tailscale ever varies the scheme or host. Low risk (the message is currently fixed), but a looser match (e.g., the "requires an additional check" line alone) would be more robust.

3. **`classifySshError` now runs on every timeout.** Setting `err.stderrKind = classifySshError(stderr)` on every timeout is negligible cost, but worth noting it's a regex pass added to an already-error path. Fine.

payload.title: fix(kanban): never auto-reclaim inline-owned running cards

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

**fix(kanban): never auto-reclaim inline-owned running cards**

Well-targeted fix with a clear ownership model. Adding `AND worker_pid IS NOT NULL` to the TTL pass in `release_stale_claims` and to `detect_stale_running` means inline owners (CLI `kanban claim` / gateway sessions, `worker_pid` NULL) are never requeued to `ready` by auto-reclaim — closing the duplicate-worker / nudge-loop cascade. Orphan reconciliation already structurally excluded inline owners (they carry `claim_lock` + `claim_expires`), so the model is internally consistent. The two tests pin both halves: inline-owned cards stay `running` (and `dispatch_once` spawns nothing), while a dead dispatcher worker is still reclaimed (crash recovery preserved).

Non-blocking observations:

1. **Stale telemetry now hides inline owners.** `detect_stale_running` also feeds `DispatchResult.stale` in `dispatch_once` (the line ~9338 call site), which is used for telemetry/monitoring. With the new filter, a genuinely hung *inline* session no longer appears in stale telemetry — it's only recoverable via operator `reclaim_task` (documented intent). If any dashboard or alert consumes `result.stale`, consider surfacing inline-owned stale cards separately (e.g., a distinct flag) so they aren't silently invisible, even though auto-reclaim correctly stays hands-off.

2. **Trivial file nit.** `tests/hermes_cli/test_kanban_inline_ownership.py` ends with "No newline at end of file". Cosmetic.

payload.author: alt-glitch
payload.body:
> *This was generated by AI during triage.*

payload.author: ttxs69
payload.body:
Acknowledged — and thanks to @cadezhou, who independently diagnosed the same silent-death root cause a month earlier in #72673. I searched for competing work before opening but missed that PR (different vocabulary: "silent death" vs "zombie/not connected").

**Relationship:** both PRs implement the same core mechanism — detached fatal-error notification so the gateway watcher takes over, with the same deadlock rationale (gateway handler → `disconnect()` → awaits `_listen_task`). The remaining delta:

| | #72673 | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| 3× reconnect-exhaustion exits | ✅ | ✅ |
| quick-disconnect exit | ✅ (added after sweeper review) | ✅ |
| fatal close-code exits (banned/offline/…) | ❌ still `_set_fatal_error` without notify → same zombie | ✅ notified, non-retryable |
| notify-task exception guard | ❌ bare `create_task(self._notify_fatal_error())` — a raising gateway handler leaves an unawaited task error and the notification is lost | ✅ guarded best-effort wrapper |
| quick-disconnect `_fail_pending` | ❌ | ✅ (defensive parity) |
| error-code context (last close code / exc) | ✅ | ✅ absorbed in 57499c3cd8, credit in commit message |
| tests | mock `_notify_fatal_error` (noted by sweeper) | real notify chain, handler calls `disconnect()` (deadlock guard), mutation-tested |

**Suggested consolidation:** take this PR as the base — it is a strict superset after absorbing the error-code context, and #72673's remaining gaps are the two real defects above (unguarded notify task, unnotified fatal-close exits). @cadezhou's authorship of the core mechanism deserves credit and is acknowledged in the commit message and PR description.

If the team prefers #72673 as the base instead, I'm happy to port the three fixes there as commits — whichever unblocks the merge fastest works for me. The bug has been live on main for a long time (we hit it in production: a 2h DNS outage on 2026-08-19 left qqbot dead for 10 days).

payload.author: rakeshr
payload.title: fix(peer): keep remote DM turns alive over SSE

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

**fix(peer): keep remote DM turns alive over SSE**

Sound switch from the buffered `/chat` route to `/chat/stream` (SSE), which is the right fix for idle-timeout drops on long peer turns: the streaming twin prepares headers immediately and emits keepalives. The hand-rolled SSE parser is careful — it accumulates `data:` lines per event, joins with `\n`, dispatches on `assistant.completed`/`error`, and resets state on blank lines. The projection back into the old `_request` result shape (`session_id` + `message.role/content`) keeps callers unchanged, and the test correctly forces the buffered route to fail-closed (500) so a regression can't silently switch back.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **The test doesn't exercise real streaming.** The fake server writes the entire SSE payload (keepalive + `assistant.completed` + `done`) in a single write with `Content-Length`, so the client likely receives it in one read. The parser is validated, but the actual property this PR targets — events arriving incrementally over time with the socket otherwise idle — is not. Consider a test that writes the keepalive, then the completed event in a second write after a small delay, to emulate incremental delivery (and confirm the socket timeout doesn't fire between frames).

2. **`DM_TIMEOUT_S` is now a per-read socket timeout, not a total deadline.** With keepalives arriving inside the window, a single peer turn can run well past `DM_TIMEOUT_S` wall-clock. That's the intended idle-timeout survival, but worth confirming the CLI UX is acceptable for a turn that can now take arbitrarily long.

3. **Empty-data edge.** If the stream ends on a `done` event without ever dispatching `assistant.completed`, `completed` stays `None` and the function raises "ended without a completed assistant response" — a clear, correct failure mode. No issue, just noting the contract.

payload.author: nftpoetrist
payload.title: fix(auth): key the global auth-store memo on content digest, not mtime

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

**fix(auth): key the global auth-store memo on content digest, not mtime**

Correct and security-relevant fix. A stat-only key genuinely cannot detect a metadata-preserving replace of `auth.json` (dotfile sync, backup/restore), and serving stale — or entirely different — global credentials indefinitely is a real credential-identity hazard. The digest key closes it, and `test_metadata_preserving_replace_is_not_served_stale` pins the exact scenario (restores both atime and mtime). The parallel to the Vertex SA cache fix is well documented.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **Double read on cache miss.** On a miss the flow reads the file once for the digest, then reads/parses it again for the store. The cost note says digest-read is noise next to the JSON parse, which is fair — but a miss now reads the file twice. If a cheap "read once, hash and parse from the same bytes" refactor is easy, it removes the only inefficiency left.

2. **Full read on every probe.** Every `/model` picker row now does a full `read_bytes()` + SHA-256 of the credentials file before the memo can answer. For a small local auth.json this is fine (and cheaper than the JSON parse, as argued), but worth remembering if the global store ever lands on a slow/remote filesystem — the per-probe cost would stop being negligible. The comment already anticipates this tradeoff; just flagging it explicitly.

payload.title: fix(state): close the SessionDB lock gate's blind spot on its own mixin files

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

**fix(state): close the SessionDB lock gate's blind spot on its own mixin files**

Good fix on both halves: the reader-writer contention change routes pure-read methods in `hermes_state_portability.py` / `hermes_state_search.py` through `_read_ctx()` instead of holding the writer lock, and the gate test now scans all four files that contribute `SessionDB` methods (`hermes_state.py` + the three mixins). The sabotage self-check that plants a locked reader in a fake mixin file is a good guard against the scope silently narrowing again.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **`_read_ctx()` semantics.** The change substitutes `conn` (from `_read_ctx()`) for `self._conn` in each body. Assuming `_read_ctx()` returns the same connection under a shared/read lock (the established Pattern-C fix), this is correct. If instead it ever returns a *different* read-only connection, methods relying on a write-consistent snapshot or on writes through that handle could silently misbehave — worth a quick confirmation that `_read_ctx()` hands back the same `self._conn` (or a coherent reader) for these queries.

2. **Hardcoded mixin file/class list in the gate.** `_ALL_STATE_SOURCES` hardcodes the three mixin file names and class names. If `SessionDB`'s inheritance changes (new mixin, renamed class), the gate could silently narrow again — exactly the failure mode this PR fixes. Consider deriving the mixin list from `SessionDB.__mro__` (or asserting the hardcoded classes are still in the MRO) so the gate fails loudly when the file set drifts. The added sabotage test helps, but only covers what the list already includes.

payload.author: BankzNNBB
payload.title: fix(cron): fire on_session_finalize when a cron job finishes

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

**fix(cron): fire on_session_finalize when a cron job finishes**

Solid fix with strong regression tests. Firing `lifecycle.finalize_session` after `end_session` and ordering it *before* `close()` (so a hook can still read session state) is the right call, and the wrapped try/except correctly guarantees the SQLite teardown always runs even when a plugin raises. The use of `_final_cron_session_id` (resolved/compression-rotated id) rather than the raw pre-agent id is well-reasoned and pinned by `test_run_job_finalizes_compression_continuation`.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **Debug-level logging of hook failures.** The `except (Exception, KeyboardInterrupt)` around the finalize call only logs at `logger.debug`. That is consistent with the surrounding teardown handlers, but a genuinely misbehaving lifecycle plugin will be effectively invisible in normal (INFO) logs — the fd-leak symptom it protects against will re-appear silently. Consider logging unexpected (non-`KeyboardInterrupt`) exceptions at WARNING while still never skipping teardown.

2. **Placement vs. failed/aborted runs.** The hunk lands after `end_session` in what appears to be the normal completion path. If a cron job fails before reaching that point (exception, interrupt, or the early `return`-style paths), `on_session_finalize` will not fire, so the "every start has a matching end" invariant claimed in the docstring may not hold for failed runs. If the intent is coverage for all terminal states, verify the finalize call also runs on the failure/abort branches (or explicitly document it as completion-only).

3. **Lazy import.** `from hermes_cli import lifecycle` inside the function is a reasonable circular-import guard, but it means a broken lifecycle import is only discovered at cron runtime, not at startup. Minor.

payload.author: SulthanZahran1
payload.title: fix(state): fail open on FTS5-index-only corruption instead of killing turns

payload.author: andrexibiza
payload.body:
Reviewed exact head `cb4333e20b3867f3d9a8ce03ee8d07279a0d8ee2` against base `57746cbb842a2e0e58734623567d25102b91db04`, plus current `main@299c652a66bcc915a2a1e10cd2b648f196ec4bba`. I read the 7-file diff, the new regression tests, #97794 and its evidence, the competing #97841 implementation, the merged #92523 salvage history, open #96038's provenance narrowing, and the adjacent #88587/#88604 doctor-side classification work.

There is good work here: moving destructive recovery advice behind a stronger structural/index distinction is the right direction, the LIKE degradation lives at the `SessionDB.search_messages` ownership boundary rather than being duplicated in every caller, and the new tests are materially stronger than marker-only coverage. I do see two blockers before this can be the `Fixes #97794` owner.

**P1 — this changes the diagnosis, but the exact turn still fail-closes.**

The only transcript-write changes in this head annotate the escaping `sqlite3.Error` with `db_path`; they do not alter the caller's stop semantics. On current main, when `_flush_messages_to_session_db(...)` fails, `agent/conversation_loop.py` records the classified cause and then unconditionally sets `_turn_exit_reason = "session_persistence_failed"`, `final_response = ""`, `failed = True`, and breaks specifically so Hermes does not execute tools from unpersisted state. `agent/turn_finalizer.py` in turn stamps every failed `session_persistence_failed` result as an error regardless of the cause. This PR does not touch either boundary.

The new explainer actually exposes the mismatch: for `fts_index` it still says **"the turn was stopped"** and **"send your message again"**. That is the original dropped-message behavior from #97794, only with safer advice. Meanwhile `gateway/run.py` says **"Messages are persisted normally"**, which cannot be true for the exact append that escaped `_execute_write` and caused the failure.

So the core issue contract — a proven FTS-only failure must not kill the turn / drop the user's message — is not yet closed. Please either:

1. make the proven-FTS-only write path recover/detach/retry through to a durable canonical commit *before* the turn continues, with a regression that proves the same user message is actually present in `messages` and the turn proceeds rather than returning `session_persistence_failed`; or
2. narrow this PR to the honest diagnosis + search-degradation slice, remove the `Fixes #97794` closure claim, and leave the turn-continuation/durability slice open for its real owner.

The second option is still valuable; it just should not launder "less destructive failure messaging" into "fail open" completion.

**P1 — the new classifier bypasses SQLite's stronger result-code provenance.**

`classify_persistence_error()` now returns `fts_index` immediately for any text containing both `fts5` and `corrupt`:

```py
if "fts5" in text and "corrupt" in text:
    return "fts_index"
```

That happens before the new database probe and without consulting `sqlite_errorcode`. #96038 is the other side of this exact shape: it demonstrates why known SQLite result codes must outrank error prose. Its regression constructs FTS-looking text paired with `SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_TRIGGER` and correctly requires fail-closed behavior; only `SQLITE_CORRUPT_VTAB` is accepted as old-SQLite FTS provenance, while bare `SQLITE_CORRUPT` / contradictory known codes are rejected. At this head, that contradictory exception would be reclassified as `fts_index` solely because its string says `fts5 ... corrupt`.

Please make the evidence order explicit and shared across the write-repair gate and the persistence classifier: known result code first (`SQLITE_CORRUPT_VTAB` is FTS-scoped; contradictory known codes fail closed), then a narrow text fallback only when no code is available and the error identifies a known `messages_fts*` object, then the canonical-table probe for generic markers. Add the contradictory-code regression here too. That keep

payload.author: Finn763
payload.title: fix(update): regenerate dangling editable finder after interrupted install on Windows

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `hermes_cli/_install_repair.py` / `_early_recovery.py` / `main.py` / `update_cmd.py` for PR #97842. The diagnosis is correct and the failure mode is nasty: an interrupted `hermes update` on Windows can leave the editable-install finder's `MAPPING` pointing at a deleted `site-packages/hermes_cli` physical copy, so `hermes.exe` dies with `ModuleNotFoundError` and the `.update-incomplete` retry never regenerates the mapping. The change adds finder-health checks + regeneration across the early-recovery, core-install, and `update --check` paths, and anchors repo detection at the install directory instead of a poisoned `site-packages` path — all reasonable.

Non-blocking observations (several worth a look given the destructive surface):

1. **`_clean_stale_site_packages_physical_copies` deletes by top-level *name* match, including generic names.** The `_HERMES_EDITABLE_FALLBACK_TOP_LEVELS` set includes `"tools"`, `"utils"`, `"cli"`, `"plugins"`, `"gateway"`, `"agent"`, `"cron"` — all extremely common third-party top-level package names. For any non-symlink directory matching one of these in `site-packages`, the code runs `shutil.rmtree(target)`. If a user has any *other* package installed that ships a top-level `tools`/`utils`/`cli`/`plugins` module, this repair step can delete it. It only runs during recovery/repair of interrupted installs, which limits blast radius, but name-matching against a hardcoded generic list is risky. Consider gating the deletion on package provenance (e.g. presence of a `hermes-agent*.dist-info`/RECORD that lists the path) before rmtree, or at minimum restrict the fallback list to clearly Hermes-specific names.

2. **`main.py`'s final guard can reference an unbound `_reasons`.** In `_recover_core_update_marker_locked`, the final guard does `_is_dangling, _ = _ir.editable_finder_is_dangling(...)` then `raise RuntimeError(f"editable finder still dangling: {_reasons}")`. `_reasons` is only bound in the *previous* try block; if that earlier call raised before assignment, the `raise` becomes a `NameError`, which is caught by `except Exception: pass` — silently defeating the guard (marker cleared despite a dangling finder). The internal implementation rarely raises, so this is an edge case, but binding `_reasons` in the guard itself (or using the second tuple element) removes the coupling.

3. **`ensure_editable_finder_health` appears to have no callers** (no references in the current tree or in the diff's hunks). If it's intended for future use, that's fine, but per the repo's dead-code guidance it's worth either wiring it in or dropping it until a consumer exists.

4. **The finder-health + regenerate pattern is duplicated across four files** (`_early_recovery.py`, `main.py`, and twice in `_install_repair.run_core_install`). Centralizing on `ensure_editable_finder_health` (or a single "verify → clean → regenerate" helper) would remove the copy-paste and the inconsistency risk (the four sites use slightly different messaging/behavior).

5. **`editable_finder_is_dangling` returns healthy when no finder files exist.** Absence of `__editable__*finder.py` is not treated as dangling, but a missing finder is equally fatal to the launcher. If the goal is full launcher health, "no finder" should probably be reported, or at least documented as out of scope.

The PR addresses a real, painful failure mode and the fallback-chain approach in `update --check` is thoughtful; the main risk to address is the name-based deletion in item 1.

payload.title: fix(state): don't fail-close turns on FTS-index-only errors

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `hermes_state.py` / `hermes_state_search.py` / `run_agent.py` / `gateway/run.py` / `tools/session_search_tool.py` (+ the new `"fts_index"` cause) for PR #97841. The design is sound and fail-safe: an FTS5-shadow-table-only error is reclassified as `fts_index` so the turn degrades to LIKE search instead of fail-closing with the destructive `.recover` guidance that applies to canonical-table corruption. The user-facing messages in `run_agent.py` and `gateway/run.py` are appropriately reassuring ("messages are still persisted and safe"). I confirmed `_search_messages_like_fallback` exists at `hermes_state_search.py:1541`, so the fallback wiring is valid.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **Message-based classification has an inherent false-positive risk.** The new branch returns `fts_index` whenever a corruption marker AND an FTS marker (`messages_fts`/`fts5`) co-occur — or more broadly when an FTS marker plus the word "corrupt" appear. A genuinely canonical corruption that happens to mention the FTS table in a traceback/context (e.g. during an FTS rebuild that itself surfaced the real damage) could be mislabeled `fts_index`, which then steers the user away from the real repair path. The downside is fail-safe (degrade to LIKE, keep the turn), so this is acceptable — but the second, looser branch (`any fts in text and "corrupt" in text`) is the most permissive and worth a closer look for false positives.

2. **`tools/session_search_tool.py` reaches into a private method via `hasattr(db, "_search_messages_like_fallback")`.** The `hasattr` guard is defensive, but coupling a tool to a private method name means a rename silently disables the fallback (falls through to `tool_error`). Consider exposing this as a public method or checking the class contract, so the fallback can't silently rot.

3. **Minor:** in `_search_messages_impl`, `_try_runtime_fts_rebuild(exc)` is attempted *before* the LIKE fallback even though the index is known corrupt; if it fails (likely), the exception is swallowed and LIKE runs anyway. Harmless (it's a best-effort self-heal), just slightly wasted work in the common corrupt case.

The change correctly implements a real degradation path and keeps user guidance non-destructive. Nothing blocking.

payload.author: Finn763
payload.title: fix(skills): detect destination drift even when source hash matches manifest

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `tools/skills_sync.py` (+ tests) for PR #97840. The fix addresses both the #97791 destination-drift blind spot and a genuine second-order bug: a stock copy that already matches bundled (e.g. manually repaired) is now re-baselined in the manifest instead of being reported as `user_modified` forever — in `sync_skills` and in `list_user_modified_bundled_skills` (which now also self-heals the manifest best-effort). The `.as_posix()` change in the test is a nice Windows portability fix.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **This overlaps heavily with #97834**, which fixes the same #97791 in the same file with a similar stat-based helper (`_stat_fingerprint` there vs `_dir_file_stats` here). The two should be reconciled rather than merged independently — #97840's additional stale-manifest self-heal is a superset that could be folded onto whichever version of the stat check lands.

2. **The fast path is no longer fast — every sync now full-hashes the destination.** In both stat branches (`count/size` equal or not), the code calls `_dir_hash(dest)` before deciding to skip. The original optimization existed specifically to avoid hashing the user's copy when the bundled source was unchanged; this PR removes that entirely, so every sync hashes all destination files for every bundled skill. On a large installed skill tree this is a real per-sync cost regression. #97834's variant keeps the fast path (stat match → skip without hashing). If the intent is "cheap-verifiable + full-hash", consider skipping the hash when stats match AND accepting the documented same-size-drift blind spot, or at least measuring the impact. The `_dir_file_stats` docstring even says "when stats match we also hash to catch same-size content drift" — that's the explicit trade-off being made, but it contradicts the "cheap pre-check" framing.

3. **The changed `test_reset_clears_stuck_user_modified_flag` now accepts both pre-fix and post-fix behavior:** if `google-workspace` lands in `user_modified` the test just `pass`es and proceeds; the self-heal assertion only runs in the `else` branch. That makes the regression test unable to *fail* on the old behavior — the "old bug" path silently passes. Recommend restructuring so the test deterministically asserts the post-fix contract (self-healed, skipped, re-baselined) and separately keeps the reset-path coverage.

Good diagnosis and the self-heal is valuable; the main items are reconciling with #97834, the perf regression, and strengthening the weakened test.

payload.author: Finn763
payload.title: fix(openrouter): strip routing suffixes before models.dev catalog lookup

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `agent/model_metadata.py` + `agent/models_dev.py` (+ tests) for PR #97839. The fix is functionally correct: routing suffixes (`:floor`, `:free`, …) are stripped before the catalog lookup so `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash:floor` resolves to the bare models.dev entry (1,310,720 instead of the hardcoded 202,752), while the full routed ID is preserved for provider requests. The candidate-list approach (bare first, stripped second) keeps the original ID authoritative. Tests cover the `get_model_context_length` path, all seven suffixes, provider-scoping, and `get_model_info` ID preservation.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **This overlaps heavily with #97837**, which fixes the same symptom in `agent/models_dev.py` (same functions: `_find_model_entry`, `lookup_models_dev_context`, `get_model_capabilities`, `get_model_info`) with a similar but differently-structured implementation. Both PRs also duplicate the routing-suffix set. Whichever lands first will conflict; the maintainers should reconcile into one implementation and one shared constant (e.g. import the set from one module rather than the "same list as agent/models_dev.py" comment in `model_metadata.py`, which will silently drift if the lists diverge).

2. **`_should_strip_openrouter_suffix` strips for ANY model when `provider is None`** (the permissive branch "so bare-model tests pass"). That changes behavior for existing direct `_find_model_entry(models, model)` callers that pass no provider: a non-OpenRouter provider whose catalog legitimately contains a model literally ending in `:free`/`:thinking`/etc. would now be aliased to the bare entry. In practice model IDs with those suffixes are OpenRouter-specific, so risk is low, but the permissive-None default is a behavior change worth a deliberate look (it exists specifically for tests).

3. **`get_model_context_length` has some redundancy:** the suffix-strip lookup is attempted twice (once in the `effective_provider == "openrouter"` block, once in a second case-insensitive fallback block). It works, but a single normalized lookup helper would be tighter and avoid the near-duplicate loops.

4. **`_is_openrouter_provider_name` is defined in `model_metadata.py` but not referenced in the diff** — if it's dead code, drop it (or wire it into the `effective_provider == "openrouter"` check for consistency with `models_dev`).

Good, well-tested fix; the actionable items are the #97837 reconciliation and the `provider is None` permissive strip.

payload.author: nftpoetrist
payload.title: fix(browser): add getResponseBodyForInterception and getResourceContent to the CDP binary-redaction table

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `tools/browser_cdp_tool.py` (+ tests) for PR #97838. This is a correct, minimal extension of the #97078 binary-redaction table: `Network.getResponseBodyForInterception` and `Page.getResourceContent` carry the same `{field, base64Encoded}` shape as the already-covered methods, so adding them to `_CDP_ALWAYS_BINARY_PATHS` closes a real redaction gap. The four tests pin both sides of the contract — base64 payloads pass through untouched (Fernet-shaped pattern can't corrupt them) while `base64Encoded: false` text still gets redacted.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **The `_CDP_FLAGGED_BINARY_PATHS` counterpart was not extended.** The diff only adds to `_CDP_ALWAYS_BINARY_PATHS`. If `Page.getResourceContent`/`Network.getResponseBodyForInterception` should also be in the "flagged" (conditional) table for some consumers, that's a separate gap; the PR description only claims the always-binary table, so this is likely intentional — worth a one-line note for completeness.

2. **Minor:** `Page.getResourceContent`'s carrier key is `content` while the others use `body` — the table correctly encodes per-method field names, and the tests confirm the right key is read. No issue.

3. **Minor:** the protocol methods added are documented/deprecated in places (`getResponseBodyForInterception` is legacy but still live per the test comment) — fine to cover; no action needed.

Small, well-tested, low-risk addition that follows the established pattern exactly. Nothing blocking.

payload.author: fangliquanflq
payload.title: fix(model-metadata): resolve routed OpenRouter context windows correctly

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `agent/models_dev.py` (+ tests) for PR #97837. The refactor from the scattered exact/case-insensitive/suffix fallbacks into `_catalog_model_id` + `_find_model_entry_with_id` is a genuine improvement: provider-aware stripping of OpenRouter routing suffixes before the catalog lookup, while preserving the full routed ID for the provider/config layer (`get_model_info` returns the routed ID). The `:cloud`/`-cloud` fallback is preserved (folded into the shared helper) so the kimi-k2.6:cloud path still works, and tests cover every documented suffix plus the provider-scoped and unknown-suffix negatives.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **This overlaps heavily with #97839, which fixes the same symptom in the same files** (`agent/models_dev.py` `_find_model_entry` / `lookup_models_dev_context` / `get_model_capabilities` / `get_model_info`, plus `agent/model_metadata.py`). #97839 also strips in `model_metadata.py`'s `get_model_context_length` directly, which #97837 does not touch (it relies on `lookup_models_dev_context` for that path). Whichever lands first will conflict with the other; the maintainers should pick one and reconcile, ideally sharing one definition of the routing-suffix set and one strip helper rather than the duplicated constants both PRs introduce.

2. **Case handling in `_catalog_model_id` is exact-lowercase for the provider id** — fine. For the suffix strip it uses `model.lower().endswith(suffix)` which is case-insensitive; note `model[: -len(suffix)]` then returns the original-case prefix (correct — preserves casing of the real model id). Good.

3. **Minor:** `_find_model_entry_with_id` returns a tuple while `_find_model_entry` unwraps it — reasonable, but the two-function split adds surface; the tests exercise both `lookup_models_dev_context` and `get_model_capabilities`/`get_model_info` through it, so coverage is adequate.

4. **Minor:** `_default_override_context(provider)` still runs when all candidate lookups miss — the routed model falling through to a hardcoded family default is now only possible when the bare entry is also absent from the catalog, which is the correct residual behavior.

Solid refactor with good tests. The only real action item is coordinating with #97839.

payload.author: fangliquanflq
payload.body:
Thanks for the detailed review. I rechecked each observation against the current head and `main`:

1. The overlap with #97839 is confirmed. #97837 remains intentionally scoped to #97820’s models.dev catalog miss. `get_model_context_length()` already falls through from an exact OpenRouter live-metadata lookup to `lookup_models_dev_context()`, where this PR performs the provider-scoped normalization. Adding the same suffix table to `model_metadata.py` would duplicate the definition without being needed for the reported catalog-backed case. Maintainers can therefore choose between the overlapping implementations; no code change is needed in this PR for coordination.
2. Confirmed: suffix matching is case-insensitive while the original model prefix is preserved.
3. Confirmed: the tuple-returning helper is used only where the matched catalog ID is required to preserve the routed provider-facing ID; other callers use the entry-only wrapper.
4. Confirmed: `_default_override_context()` remains a catalog-miss fallback and cannot preempt a routed model whose bare catalog entry exists.

Evidence: `tests/agent/test_models_dev.py` covers all documented suffixes, provider scoping, unknown suffixes, capabilities, and routed-ID preservation; `tests/agent/test_model_metadata.py` exercises the full context-resolution path through the models.dev fallback. At head `3fe122df177549ed3f67eb552187a2f2e7f07ffb`, both “Python tests / Run tests” and “All required checks pass” are successful.

payload.author: will-lynas
payload.title: fix(slack): sanitize resolved clarify message blocks

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `plugins/platforms/slack/adapter.py` (+ test) for PR #97836. Applying the existing `sanitize_blocks()` boundary to resolved clarification-card updates is the minimal, correct fix: Slack's interaction payload can re-escape the question text (e.g. `&` → `&`), pushing the blocks past the 3,000-char / `MAX_SECTION_TEXT` limit and causing `invalid_blocks` on `chat.update`. The regression test is well constructed — it drives the re-escaped question past `MAX_SECTION_TEXT`, verifies the actions block is removed on resolution, and asserts the updated section text is back within the limit.

Non-blocking observation:

- **Verify `sanitize_blocks` is already imported in `adapter.py`.** The diff only adds the call site, not the import. If the module-level import already exists (it's described as an existing shared helper used elsewhere in the file), no action needed; if not, the module won't compile. Worth a quick confirm.
- **Minor:** the fix sanitizes `updated_blocks` but leaves `decision_text` (the plain-text `text=` argument to `chat_update`) unsanitized. If the re-escaped text is also passed there it's not subject to the Block Kit limit, so this is fine — just confirming the text path was intentionally left as-is.

Small, well-targeted fix with a precise regression test. Nothing blocking.

payload.author: nftpoetrist
payload.title: fix(profiles): make_targz writes to a temp file and renames, not the destination directly

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `hermes_cli/archive_safe.py` (+ new tests) for PR #97835. Converting `make_targz` to write a sibling temp file and `os.replace` only on success is the correct failure-atomicity fix: `tarfile.open(path, "w:gz")` truncates the destination on open, so a mid-`add` failure previously destroyed any pre-existing archive. The temp file is placed in the destination directory (same filesystem, so `os.replace` is atomic) and is cleaned up on failure — including the `BaseException` catch which covers interruption. Tests pin all three contracts: failure preserves the sentinel, success round-trips content, and success overwrites.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **`os.replace` atomicity relies on the temp file being on the same filesystem as `archive_path`** — it is (same directory via `mkstemp(dir=dest_dir)`), so this is solid. If `base` ever points across volumes, `os.replace` would fail and `make_targz` would raise after having written a valid temp file that gets unlinked in the `except` — acceptable, but the unlink-on-`os.replace`-failure path is worth a glance.

2. **Minor:** the temp file name carries `.tar.gz.tmp` (plus a random suffix); if a crash happens between `mkstemp` and the `try` body, an orphaned `.archive_*` file could remain (the `try/except BaseException` only covers the write+rename block). The test asserts no leftovers *after a handled failure*, which is the contract that matters; an abrupt process kill is inherently un-cleanable in-process.

3. **Minor:** `make_targz`'s caller-facing behavior is unchanged (same return value and same final artifact), so the two consumers (`profile export`, `kanban export`) need no updates — good.

Clean, well-scoped change with a real safety improvement. Nothing blocking.

payload.author: liuhao1024
payload.title: fix(skills): verify destination integrity before the unchanged-source skip

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `tools/skills_sync.py` (+ tests) for PR #97834. The fast-path fix is exactly right: the unchanged-source skip (`bundled_hash == origin_hash`) now gated on a cheap `_stat_fingerprint` (file count + total size) so destination drift that never touches the bundled source surfaces instead of being masked as "up to date" forever (#97791). The tests pin both directions — drifted destination flagged as `user_modified`, and a healthy second sync still skipped with no noise.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **Competing/overlapping fix — #97840 addresses the same #97791 in the same file.** Both introduce a near-identical stat helper (`_stat_fingerprint` here vs `_dir_file_stats` there) and both restructure the same fast-path block in `sync_skills`. Whichever merges first will likely conflict with the other; the maintainers should reconcile them (pick one helper + one self-heal strategy, or fold #97840's stale-manifest re-baseline in on top of this one) rather than merge both as-is.

2. **A stat match still skips without a content hash — correct for perf, with a known trade-off.** Two trees with identical file count+size but different content (same-size content drift) would still be treated as "up to date". #97840's variant always hashes the destination (no fast-path savings); this PR keeps the fast path but accepts the same-size-drift blind spot. Given the bug being fixed is about *missing/moved files* (structural drift), the count+size fingerprint covers the reported class; a comment noting the same-size limitation would help.

3. **Minor:** `_stat_fingerprint` returns `None` on scan error, and the caller treats that as "fingerprints disagree" (safe fallback to full hash) — good defensive choice. The `rglob` + `stat` cost is bounded and runs only when the manifest hash matches.

The fix is minimal, well-tested, and preserves the perf intent of the fast path. The only real action item is coordinating with #97840.

payload.author: forumevi
payload.title: test: fix mock type errors and sync call handling in conversation loop edge cases

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `tests/test_conversation_loop_edge_cases.py` for PR #97828. The fixture correctly initializes the numeric session/iteration counters (`_skill_nudge_interval`, `_iters_since_skill`, etc.) that previously left MagicMock unconfigured, and the tests target `run_conversation`'s `moa_config` / `stream_callback=None` edge handling. I confirmed `run_conversation` in `agent/conversation_loop.py` is a plain (synchronous) `def`, so calling it synchronously in the tests is valid.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **The assertions are weak — `assert result is not None`.** Because `run_conversation` is synchronous, the code path does execute, but "not None" would pass for a wide range of wrong behavior. If the intent is to pin "invalid moa_config does not crash and returns a usable result", assert something stronger about the result shape (e.g. a key like `final_response` or a status field) rather than only non-None.

2. **The first test's try/except pattern masks failures:** `except Exception as e: pytest.fail(...)` re-raises as a failure, which is fine, but the `for config in invalid_configs` loop means a crash in an earlier iteration still reports the later iteration correctly — acceptable. More notably, if `run_conversation` returns a coroutine-free dict but the mocked `agent` doesn't actually exercise the moa_config branch (the fixture's `_ra` patch replaces `agent.conversation_loop._ra`), the test may pass without exercising the real invalid-config path. payload.title: fix(update_cmd): self-heal first-party modules deleted by stash restore (#97787)

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `hermes_cli/update_cmd.py` for PR #97821. The self-heal is a sensible response to the #97787 failure mode: when `git stash apply` re-applies a pre-update deletion of a file the update just pulled in, restoring it from `HEAD` before falling through to the warning is the right narrow fix, and re-validating the import after the restore is the correct success gate.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **The restore only covers dotted module paths (`"." in failing_module`).** `hermes_cli.tools_config` → `hermes_cli/tools_config.py` works, but the critical-modules list also contains top-level modules with no dot — `run_agent`, `model_tools`, `toolsets` — which would produce `run_agent.py` etc. via the same deletion-and-stash-restore path and would NOT trigger this self-heal (the `"." in failing_module` guard skips them). If a deleted top-level module is the #97787 shape too, the same `git checkout HEAD -- <path>.py` logic would apply to `failing_module + ".py"`; consider handling the no-dot case as well, or documenting that the self-heal intentionally covers only package modules.

2. **`git checkout HEAD -- <module_path>` runs with `cwd=_m().PROJECT_ROOT` and a path derived from the module name** — not user input, so traversal risk is low. But it will also "restore" a file that the update legitimately *renamed* (the path may simply not exist at HEAD under the old name), in which case the checkout returns non-zero and is safely skipped. Fine.

3. **Minor:** after a successful restore the code only prints the "Restored missing … from HEAD" message; it doesn't re-run any syntax validation beyond the import re-check. Since `_validate_critical_files_syntax` was likely already done earlier in the flow, this is acceptable.

The fix is small, targeted, and addresses the reported crash. Nothing blocking.

payload.title: fix(gateway): handle missing unix server on Windows

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `gateway/shutdown_watchdog.py` (+ tests) for PR #97817. The intent — stop the noisy `AttributeError`/warning traceback on native Windows while keeping real bind failures diagnostic on supported platforms — is right, and the two regression tests correctly pin the no-warning path and the still-warns bind-failure path.

One evidence-based caveat worth verifying before relying on it:

- **`hasattr(asyncio, "start_unix_server")` only covers Python versions where the attribute is genuinely absent.** I verified on this Windows box with Python 3.14.7: `hasattr(asyncio, "start_unix_server")` is `False`, so the guard works there. But on older CPython versions (roughly ≤3.12) the module-level function is present and only fails at call time — `loop.start_unix_server(...)` raises `NotImplementedError` (and some loops raise `AttributeError`) when awaited. In that case `hasattr` returns `True`, the new branch is skipped, and the exact startup warning this PR intends to remove still fires on those Pythons.
- Suggested hardening (cheap): in addition to (or instead of) the `hasattr` check, treat `NotImplementedError` / `AttributeError` from the bind attempt as a platform-fail-safe too — e.g. broaden the `except Exception` around `start_unix_server` to detect `NotImplementedError` and log at `info` instead of `warning`. That makes the behavior version-independent rather than relying on the attribute being present/absent.

The tests themselves are good (the `monkeypatch.delattr(...)` and the failing-bind monkeypatch both exercise the branch logic deterministically). Non-blocking, but if the gateway targets the 3.11/3.12 range on Windows, the current guard may not achieve its stated goal on those versions.

payload.author: Enough1122

> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `tools/project_tools.py` + `tui_gateway/server.py` + tests for PR #97814. Making the workspace-move outcome explicit (`moved: bool` + truthful `warning`) is the right fix for the silent "DB updated, chat not moved" case, and the legacy-`None`-callback handling (`result is not False`) preserves back-compat cleanly. The `_finalized` skip in `_apply_project_workspace` (moving only a live session, not a finalized one) is a sensible refinement and is covered by tests.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **`_apply_workspace` treats any callback return other than `False` as "moved"** (`result is not False`). A callback that returns `0`/`''`/`None` is read as success — intended for legacy `None`, but it also silently swallows a buggy callback that returns a falsy non-`None`. Strictly, `is True` would be more precise, though the legacy-`None` contract documented in the diff justifies the current choice. Worth a one-line comment that only explicit `False` means "not moved".

2. **`_apply_workspace` returns `False` when `path` is falsy**, which is what produces the "no folder" warning — but it also returns `False` on any callback exception (swallowing `Exception`). That means a transient failure inside the gateway callback is reported to the user as "live chat workspace could not be moved" — accurate, but the original `pass`-and-succeed behavior (DB-only success) is now a hard failure signal. Fine for truthfulness; just confirming the intended trade-off (a callback hiccup now surfaces as `moved: false` + warning rather than silent DB-only success).

3. **Minor:** `_find_live_session_by_key` is referenced by `_apply_project_workspace`; it exists in `tui_gateway/server.py` (confirmed in the current tree), so the wiring is valid. The direct-key lookup now also checks `_finalized` before preferring a matching live session — covered by `test_project_workspace_callback_skips_finalized_session_for_live_continuation`.

The change is small, truthful, and well-tested. Nothing blocking.

Reviewed `apps/desktop/src/lib/todos.ts` (+ `use-message-stream` integration + tests) for PR #97811. The fix correctly models the two write semantics: a full `payload.todos` / `result` replaces the list, while `args.merge === true` patches by id. payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `apps/desktop/src/plugins/hermes-bots/group-hold-status.tsx` (+ view integration + i18n + tests) for PR #97808. The approach is sound: projecting the durable `room.holds` map into a `role="status"` row keeps the explanation alive across run/epoch reloads, and the tests pin the all-held, partial, source-qualified, and hydrated-workspace cases. i18n coverage across all four shipped locales is complete.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **Member↔hold matching relies entirely on `groupMemberKey` producing the same key shape the hold map uses.** The component splits `key.split('::')` only for *unmatched* keys (the `unavailableHeldLabels` path), so if `groupMemberKey(member)` ever emits an unqualified name (`builder`) while a persisted hold is source-qualified (`mac-mini::builder`) — or vice versa — the same bot can appear twice (once as a held member, once in the "unavailable" list). The tests cover all-unqualified and all-unqualified-absent but not the mixed case where a member row exists under a different key form than the hold. Worth one test asserting the "held member present + source-qualified hold for the same bot" display, or a comment documenting why `groupMemberKey` and hold keys are guaranteed identical.

2. **Minor:** the `allHeld` branch depends on `props.members.length > 0` and `unavailableHeldLabels.length === 0`. A fully-held room whose holds are all source-qualified while `members` is populated would render "Paused: …" rather than "All N bots are paused". Cosmetic only.

payload.author: ahaone
payload.title: fix(delegation): size child context files by model window

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `tools/delegate_tool.py` + tests for PR #97807. The change sizes delegated child context-file loading by the child's actual model window: `_build_child_system_prompt` gains a `context_length` parameter forwarded to `build_context_files_prompt`, and `_build_child_agent` resolves it *after* constructing the child — preferring the child compressor's `context_length` (strict `type(...) is int and > 0`, which correctly excludes `bool` and `0`), falling back to `get_model_context_length` metadata, then `None` (original behavior) on failure. The two-stage prompt build (bootstrap without workspace context, then `setattr(child, "ephemeral_system_prompt", ...)` with the resolved length) is a sensible chicken-and-egg solution since the child's real window is only known post-construction. Tests cover explicit forwarding, compressor-priority (metadata not called), invalid-compressor fallback, and metadata-failure → `None`.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **The first-stage prompt is constructed and then immediately replaced.** `_build_child_system_prompt(goal, context, role=..., ...)` is built *without* `workspace_path`/`context_length` and passed into `AIAgent(...)` construction, then `ephemeral_system_prompt` is overwritten with the second-stage prompt. If `AIAgent.__init__` uses the passed `ephemeral_system_prompt` for anything cached (token estimation, prompt-cache key derivation, logging) rather than only reading it later, the overwrite could leave that derived state inconsistent. The tests assert the *kwargs* prompt lacks `project-context-` but don't verify `AIAgent` never uses the first prompt after construction. Worth a comment in `_build_child_agent` (or a check) confirming the first prompt is purely a bootstrap that is never consumed post-init.
2. **`setattr(child, "ephemeral_system_prompt", ...)` bypasses any setter/hook.** Direct attribute assignment on the `AIAgent` instance. If `ephemeral_system_prompt` is read at session/agent start via a property or requires invalidation of derived state, a plain `setattr` could silently diverge. Given the existing code already treats it as a plain attribute, this is consistent — just noting the overwrite is intentionally low-level.
3. **Metadata fallback can be a network/slow call per delegated child.** `get_model_context_length(model, base_url=..., api_key=..., provider=...)` is invoked when the child compressor lacks a valid length. If that function ever performs a remote catalog lookup, it now runs once per child spawn instead of being resolved from the compressor. From the tests it behaves as a deterministic lookup, so likely fine — worth confirming it's cache-backed to avoid per-delegation latency on large batch spawns.
4. **Minor:** `type(compressor_length) is int` also rejects `numpy.int64` or other int-like values a compressor might return; consistent with the strict-typing choice, but a `numbers.Integral` check would be more forgiving if a compressor ever yields a non-`int` numeric type.

Clean, well-tested sizing fix; nothing blocking.

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `tests/hermes_cli/test_colors.py` (new) for PR #97806. The tests correctly pin the *behavior* of `hermes_cli.colors` — `NO_COLOR`, `TERM=dumb`, non-TTY disabling, and code application/concatenation — rather than the internals of every call site. Using a `StringIO` for non-TTY and a `_Tty(StringIO)` subclass for TTY is a clean, hermetic way to exercise the gating without a real terminal. Adding the first direct coverage for a module imported by ~20 files is genuinely valuable.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **`test_should_use_color_no_color_takes_precedence_over_tty` doesn't test what its name claims.** It sets `NO_COLOR` + `StringIO` (non-TTY) and asserts `False` — but non-TTY already yields `False`, so this test would pass even if `NO_COLOR` were ignored entirely. The actual precedence claim ("NO_COLOR beats a TTY") needs a `_Tty` + `NO_COLOR` case asserting `False` (mirroring how `test_color_applies_codes_when_color_enabled` fakes a TTY). As written, the name overstates the coverage.
2. **`test_colors_constants_are_ansi_escapes` asserts literal escape values.** `Colors.RED == "\x1b[31m"` pins a specific value. The ANSI SGR sequences are a stable standard, so this won't break on routine data changes (not a classic change-detector test), but it is a snapshot of the constant values rather than behavior — if the module ever mapped colors to named aliases or offered a `Colors`-by-name lookup, a behavior-level assertion would be stronger. Acceptable as a documented contract.
3. **Minor:** all tests rely on `monkeypatch.setattr("hermes_cli.colors.sys.stdout", ...)`; if `should_use_color()` is ever refactored to read stdout through a helper or to cache its result, several tests would silently no-op. payload.author: JoaoMarcos44
payload.title: fix(desktop): restore Windows Explorer file drops

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `apps/desktop/src/app/chat/composer/inline-refs.ts`, `use-composer-drop.ts`, `use-file-drop-zone.ts`, `user-edit-composer.tsx` + tests for PR #97805. The fix is well-designed and thoroughly tested: a stateful `createDragLifecycleGate` (unit-testable, held in a `useRef`) arms on the first credible signal — a typed file drag *or* a fully-empty `DataTransfer` (the Windows Explorer / Chromium sparse case) — and keeps `dragover` accepting for that drag so the app-lifetime react-dnd HTML5Backend's capture-time `dropEffect='none'` can't suppress the eventual drop. The "reject a dragover with no prior dragenter" invariant prevents blanket-classifying every empty transfer, and the drop handler still verifies `extractDroppedFiles(...).length > 0`. The test suite (unit gates + two integration harnesses + enabled:false + re-drag) is exemplary.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **"Fully-empty transfer == external file drag" is a heuristic, not a fact.** `isSparseExternalFileDrag` relies on the assumption that every *internal* drag carries at least `text/plain` or `HERMES_PATHS_MIME`. That holds for in-app drags, but an empty native transfer from a non-Explorer source (e.g. some other OS's shell / a third-party app drag that populates `files` only at drop) would also arm the gate and flash the "files" overlay. The drop-time `extractDroppedFiles` guard prevents false ingestion, so this is cosmetic-only risk — but the docstring could be explicit that the sparse signal is Windows-specific and only *tentatively* implies a file drag (it says "credible signal, not proof" already — good).
2. **No staleness bound on an armed gate.** Once armed, the gate stays armed until `onLeave(true)` / `reset()` / the next `dragenter` at depth 0. If a browser ever stops delivering the terminating `drop`/`dragleave` for a drag (tab lost focus mid-drag, an extension intercepting events), the gate could stay armed and a later unrelated dragover would be accepted. In practice `dragleave` fires on exit, so this is theoretical; a time-based TTL on the armed state would be belt-and-braces. Non-blocking.
3. **Redundant disarm in `use-file-drop-zone.onDragLeave`.** At root depth it calls `gate.onLeave(true)` and then `reset()`, which itself calls `gate.reset()` — two disarms of the same gate. Harmless, just redundant.

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `hermes_cli/proxy/adapters/base.py`, `hermes_cli/proxy/adapters/nous_portal.py`, `hermes_cli/proxy/server.py` + tests for PR #97804. The design is clean: a new `upstream_headers` property on the adapter ABC declares provider-required request headers, and `_apply_upstream_headers` applies them over the filtered client set *before* the proxy's own `Authorization`, with case-insensitive key matching so a lowercase `user-agent` from the client collapses into the single adapter value instead of forwarding two duplicate headers upstream. The Nous adapter returns `HermesAgent/<version>` to satisfy the Portal's Cloudflare policy (the same class as the `/v1/models` fix in #12999). Tests cover override, no-override passthrough, and the adapter declaration.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **The override removes the downstream client's identity fingerprint unconditionally.** Every client behind this proxy (SDK, MCP server, scripts) is now identified upstream as `HermesAgent/<version>`, regardless of what it sets. That's the intent (avoid the Cloudflare 403), but it also means upstream analytics/auditing can no longer distinguish real client types, and any client that *deliberately* sets a UA (e.g. for platform gating) silently loses it. The docstring documents the override behavior; just flagging the trade-off is real and applies to all traffic through the Nous proxy.
2. **`from hermes_cli import __version__` runs on every request.** `upstream_headers` is a property evaluated per forwarded request, and the import is inside it. A module-level lazy cache (or memoized property) would avoid the import cost per request — minor, since `import` is cached after first load, but the attribute-lookup + try/except per request is unnecessary.
3. **Duplicate-case overrides within the adapter dict itself aren't collapsed.** `_apply_upstream_headers` collapses case variants from the *client* set (`out = {k: v for k, v in forwarded.items() if k.lower() not in overridden}`), but `out.update(overrides)` copies the adapter's keys verbatim — if an adapter ever declared `{"User-Agent": ..., "user-agent": ...}`, both would be forwarded as duplicates. No current adapter does this, so it's theoretical; a `lower()`-keyed dict comprehension on `overrides` would make it bulletproof.
4. **Minor:** `_v = "0"` fallback on import failure produces `HermesAgent/0` — fine as a degraded identity, but a static literal like `HermesAgent/unknown` would be clearer in logs.

Solid, minimal, and well-tested; nothing blocking.

payload.author: andrexibiza
payload.body:
Reviewed exact head `08423d89e377d9d648376abe13666a74d9e5a080` against its exact parent/current `main` `aff5125f8edf5095aef5d3d79bbbb101c95b9413`.

This clean 10-path replacement materially improves the old review surface. I rechecked the authority failures previously found on #90883 rather than carrying them forward by inertia: malformed/stale protected `SessionWritePolicy` now refuses the real turn before conversation dispatch, the relay/task lifecycle is balanced in the executable witness, self-improvement writes consume the retained `Decision` instead of re-sampling process environment, and suggestion provenance lookup now fails closed. Those repairs are real and should be preserved.

I found one new P1 at the terminal boundary.

### P1 — the protected `DENY_ALL` terminal allowlist still admits commands that mutate through command flags

`_is_provably_read_only_command()` rejects shell redirection/compound syntax, then treats any `git diff ...` invocation as read-only solely from the first two argv tokens:

```py
return len(words) >= 2 and words[0] == "git" and words[1] in {
    "diff", "log", "show", "status",
}
```

That is not enough to prove absence of mutation. Git itself has an output-writing option:

```sh
git diff --output=/tmp/sentinel
```

No rejected shell metacharacter is involved, so this passes `_is_provably_read_only_command()`. I reproduced the command in a fresh temporary repository with one modified tracked file: `git diff --output=sentinel` returned successfully and created an 85-byte `sentinel` file containing the diff.

That means a turn carrying `SessionWritePolicy.deny_all(...)` can still write an arbitrary filesystem path through `terminal_tool`, even though this PR correctly blocks the corresponding `write_file` and `patch` mutation surfaces. This is the other side of the authority shape: shell syntax may be read-only-looking while the admitted program+options still own a write effect.

Required repair: do not classify a command as "provably read-only" from the verb/subcommand alone. For every admitted command, either constrain the option grammar to a reviewed non-mutating subset or route through a stronger semantic classifier that rejects program-level output/write options before spawn. At minimum, add an executable regression under `SessionWritePolicy.deny_all(...)` for `git diff --output=<sentinel>` and prove the terminal result is blocked and the sentinel does not exist. The existing tests cover `>`, `>>`, `&&`, `;`, `||`, and pipes, and positively admit `git diff --stat`; they do not exercise this option-level mutation class.
