1. **Compaction items still never carry an id, and the compaction-with-id pairing is untested.** In the replay loop, `replay_item["id"] = norm_id` is gated on `is_ordinary`, so a compaction checkpoint with an `id` still has it stripped. The only compaction test (`test_compaction_item_does_not_affect_ordinary_reasoning_identity`) uses a compaction item *without* an id, so the exact failure class this PR guards against (id'd following item + id-less preceding reasoning/compaction → orphaned 400) is not covered for the compaction variant. If the identity rule also applies to compaction→message pairing (both are "pre-message" items in the graph), stripping the compaction id could re-open #97427 in the compaction path. Worth an explicit test with a compaction item carrying an id + a following message with an id.
2. **`reasoning_identity_intact` counts "replayed with a valid id" but not "accepted by the endpoint".** The count is a local structural check; nothing verifies the endpoint actually honors the replayed ids (e.g. if the server no longer has them cached and treats them as unknown). That's inherently unverifiable pre-flight, and the symmetric-strip fallback still prevents the *hard* 400 — just noting the assumption is documented behavior, not a guarantee.
3. **The preflight layer re-adds ids without graph awareness (documented), so it must never be the first normalizer.** `_preflight_codex_input_items`'s new docstring correctly states it does not re-infer identity graphs. If any caller ever feeds preflight raw items directly (bypassing `_chat_messages_to_responses_input`), a message-with-id + reasoning-without-id input would still hit the 400. The end-to-end test exercises converter→preflight; a unit asserting the converter is always in the wire path (or a guard in preflight) would lock that invariant.
4. **Minor:** the ordinary-reasoning classification loop and the replay loop both iterate `raw_sidecar_items` with the same filter — could be a single pass, but the two-pass shape keeps the diff readable. Cosmetic only.

The core fix is correct, the degradation is symmetric, and coverage is excellent; nothing blocking.

payload.author: tachyon-r
payload.title: fix(gateway): bound and secure launchd stdio logs

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `hermes_cli/gateway.py`, `hermes_cli/stderr_timestamp.py` + tests for PR #97776. The change correctly addresses launchd's append-only, umask-0644, non-rotating stdio handles: the plist now points `StandardOutPath`/`StandardErrorPath` at `/dev/null` and sets `Umask 63` (0o77), while the wrapper (`stderr_timestamp`) captures raw stdout/stderr into owner-only (0600), size-bounded rotating files (`gateway.stdout.log` + timestamped `gateway.error.log`). `_RotatingWriter` is solidly hardened — `O_NOFOLLOW`/`O_CLOEXEC`, `fchmod(0600)`, immediate pruning of stale backups, and `backup_count == 0` unlink path. Tests cover stdout/stderr separation, rotation bounds, backup pruning, mode tightening, and the plist assertions.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **`Umask 63` affects the whole child process, not just the log files.** The gateway process (and anything it spawns) now runs with umask 0o77, so files the gateway creates without an explicit mode become 0600 rather than 0644. For secret-bearing files that's good; but if any gateway-created file is meant to be group/shared-readable (e.g. a socket or shared config consumed by a same-group tool), it silently changes. The log files themselves are secured by explicit `fchmod`/`O_NOFOLLOW` anyway, so the umask is belt-and-braces with broader side effects — worth confirming it's intended process-wide, or narrowing it.
2. **`gateway.stdout.log` is a new file name; `gateway.log` no longer receives raw stdout on these paths.** `hermes logs gateway` and `hermes_cli/logs.py` still read the *structured* `gateway.log` (written by the logging FileHandler, unchanged), so the documented command keeps working — but operators who previously tailed `gateway.log` and saw raw stdout mixed in will now find raw prints only in `gateway.stdout.log`. A doc/message note pointing at the new file would prevent "my logs look empty" confusion.
3. **Tautological guard in `_prune_and_secure_backups`:** `candidate.name == f"{prefix}{suffix}"` where `suffix = candidate.name.removeprefix(prefix)` is always true — the real filter is `suffix.isdigit()`. Harmless, but the expression reads as if it does something; a leftover from an earlier iteration. Cosmetic.
4. **Single oversized line can exceed `max_bytes`** (rotation is between writes only) — explicitly documented in the `_RotatingWriter` docstring and consistent with `RotatingFileHandler`. Fine.
5. **`stream.tell()` on append-mode is relied on for rotation sizing.** With `buffering=0` this is reliable (position = end after each write), and the `stream.tell() and ...` short-circuit correctly skips rotation on the first write to an empty file. No issue — just noting the assumption is implicitly exercised and covered by the 32-byte rotation test.

The launchd logging contract is genuinely improved; nothing blocking.

payload.author: ricardosalta
payload.title: fix(gateway): honor --global in reasoning picker

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `gateway/slash_commands.py` + tests for PR #97775. The root fix is the `if not raw_args:` → `if not args:` change: `args` is empty after `_parse_reasoning_command_args` strips a bare `--global` (both ASCII and em-dash forms), so a flag-only global invocation now correctly opens the picker instead of falling into the typed-arg path. The multiplex-scope plumbing is also right: `_command_profile_home` is resolved once at command time (so a *delayed* picker tap writes to the originating profile, not wherever the process scope is at tap time), and the picker callback now forwards `persist_global` — a real gap, since the picker path previously never persisted globally. Tests cover both flag spellings, global persistence, and the named-profile isolation (including a delayed tap after `_profile_runtime_scope` exits).

Non-blocking observations:

1. **Override-clearing happens on `session_key`, which is profile-scoped, but the write target is `config_home`.** In the multiplex delayed-tap case, `_apply_reasoning_selection` clears `_session_reasoning_overrides[session_key]` and calls `_evict_cached_agent(session_key)` while writing config to the originating profile home. If the tap fires after the multiplex has switched the active profile, `session_key` may belong to the *other* profile — the config write lands correctly in the originating profile, but the override/cache eviction may target the wrong session. The test covers the write target but not this cross-profile eviction edge. Worth confirming the session-key is always the originating profile's key in the delayed-tap path.
2. **`_command_profile_home` is resolved before the override key is derived but only under `multiplex_profiles`.** `_resolve_profile_home_for_source(event.source)` is skipped when multiplex is off, so non-multiplexed deployments always write to `_hermes_home` — correct. Just noting the asymmetry is intentional and documented by the guard.
3. **A failed global save silently downgrades to a session override.** In `_apply_reasoning_selection`, if `_save_gateway_config_key(..., config_home=...)` returns False (e.g. the profile's config.yaml is unwritable), the code falls through to the session-override path with no signal to the user. Pre-existing behavior, but with `config_home` now pointing at an arbitrary profile the failure mode is more likely to be hit; a hint on the False branch would help diagnose a locked-down profile.

Correct fix with good regression coverage; nothing blocking.

payload.author: Dejmacro
payload.title: feat(discord): add profile-scoped voice auto-join

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `plugins/platforms/discord/adapter.py`, `gateway/run.py`, `gateway/config.py`, new `tests/gateway/test_discord_voice_auto_join.py` + docs for PR #97774. The opt-in, disabled-by-default voice auto-join is well-contained: it fires only on a non-recovered live guild message when `voice_auto_join` is enabled for the profile, joins the sender's current VC, re-binds the text channel/source, and notifies the runner to enable persisted voice mode + auto-TTS. Tests cover config seeding, the real loader, profile-over-env precedence, env-snapshot support, bind+notify, disabled-no-probe, and the runner callback.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **No short-circuit when the bot is already in that guild's voice channel.** `maybe_auto_join_voice` runs `get_user_voice_channel` (a Discord API member lookup) on every admitted live guild message even when the bot is already in the same guild VC with the same text channel bound. On a busy guild that's one API call per message and a repeated `join_voice_channel`/`_reset_voice_timeout` per message. A cheap early return (e.g. `if self._voice_text_channels.get(guild_id) == int(text_channel_id) and self.is_in_voice_channel(guild_id): return True`) would cut the per-message load with no behavior change.
2. **The auto-join path is gated only by "non-recovered guild message", not by the author.** Any admitted member's message (subject to whatever admission rules apply before `_handle_message`) can pull the bot into their VC. That's the stated design ("smaller engagement-on-message"), and it's opt-in per profile, but it means a single user can repeatedly relocate the bot (e.g. join/leave VCs and message) — consider a rate limit / cooldown or restricting to users who can already control the bot (allowlist), especially on public servers. Non-blocking.
3. **Every auto-join can persist voice mode.** `_handle_voice_joined` writes `_voice_mode` via `_save_voice_modes()` when the mode isn't already `"all"`. If a user leaves and rejoins VCs repeatedly, this is a disk write per transition. Minor, but a guard that skips the save when the mode is already `"all"` is already present (`if ... != "all"`), so it's only the first transition per chat — fine.
4. **`_apply_yaml_config` bridges to `DISCORD_VOICE_AUTO_JOIN` env even when `_skip_env_bridge` is unset but the env is already populated.** The bridge sets `os.environ["DISCORD_VOICE_AUTO_JOIN"] = str(voice_auto_join).lower()` only when the env isn't already set — good, preserves an explicit env override. The `_skip_env_bridge` guard adds a second exit. Consistent with the allow_dms PR's approach.

The core flow is correct and well-tested; nothing blocking.

payload.author: Dejmacro
payload.title: fix(dashboard): forward startup query to chat PTY

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `hermes_cli/web_server.py` + tests for PR #97773. Forwarding the authenticated WebSocket `query` param into the dashboard chat PTY's env is a clean, well-scoped fix: `_resolve_chat_argv` now pops any inherited `HERMES_TUI_QUERY` before setting the per-PTY one (preventing a stale service-level value from leaking into unrelated PTYs), the async resolver threads the param through, and the WS handler trims and caps it at 4000 chars. Tests cover the sync resolver env injection and the WS→resolver hand-off (including whitespace trimming).

Non-blocking observations:

1. **`_resolve_chat_argv` is dashboard-only, so the unconditional `env.pop` is safe.** Confirmed `_resolve_chat_argv`/`_resolve_chat_argv_async` are used only by the web-server PTY path (the CLI/TUI uses `_make_tui_argv` directly), so always popping `HERMES_TUI_QUERY` can't strip a user-set seed from a non-dashboard path. Good.
2. **Cap is applied in `pty_ws`, not at the resolver.** `query = (...)[:4000]` in `pty_ws`, while `_resolve_chat_argv` sets `env["HERMES_TUI_QUERY"] = query` unguarded. Any future caller of `_resolve_chat_argv` that passes an unbounded `query` would bypass the cap. Since the param already has a `:4000` ceiling at the single call site today this is fine — just worth a comment or a `[:4000]` at the env-set site so the invariant is enforced where it matters.
3. **Empty/whitespace query is dropped at the WS layer but `pop` still runs in the resolver.** `("" or None)` → no `query` kwarg → `env.pop("HERMES_TUI_QUERY")` still executes, which is exactly the intended "no stale seed" behavior. Consistent.
4. **Minor:** `_resolve_chat_argv_async` only forwards `query` when truthy; a caller passing an intentionally empty string to *clear* an inherited query would get the pop path via the sync resolver anyway, so no behavioral gap.

Correct, minimal, and well-tested; nothing blocking.

payload.author: Dejmacro
payload.title: feat(camofox): support external noVNC discovery

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `tools/browser_camofox.py` + tests + docs for PR #97772. The refactor is clean: health check and VNC discovery are now decoupled, the legacy `/health` `vncPort` path is preserved, Camofox 1.13's `/vnc/status` is consulted as an optional fallback, and both `browser.camofox.vnc_url` config and the legacy `CAMOFOX_VNC_URL` env bridge are honored with explicit config precedence. `_validated_vnc_url` and `_discovered_vnc_url` are good hardening (scheme/hostname/port bounds, IPv6 brackets, path validation), and tests cover config-over-env, legacy env, and the optional-endpoint-failure case.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **`_get_camofox_config()` / `get_secret()` now run outside the exception guard.** The old function wrapped its whole body in `try/except Exception: return False`; the refactor only guards the `requests.get` and the two JSON-parsing blocks. `_get_camofox_config()` and `get_secret("CAMOFOX_VNC_URL", "")` run in the `if not _vnc_url_checked` block with no guard, so a config-loading or secret-file error would now propagate instead of returning `False`. Callers presumably treat this as a pure boolean probe — consider wrapping the whole discovery block (or at least `_get_camofox_config`) so health probing can't throw.
2. **The `_vnc_url_checked` cache is never invalidated.** Once set, the discovered URL is cached for process lifetime. If the Camofox server restarts on a different port or the operator changes `browser.camofox.vnc_url` at runtime, `get_vnc_url()` keeps returning the stale value. This matches the prior behavior (cache existed before), so it's not a regression — just noting the explicit `vnc_url` config would still require a restart to take effect.
3. **Path is not URL-encoded and may carry no query.** `_discovered_vnc_url` accepts any `path` starting with `/` (and not `//`), so a Camofox-returned path containing spaces or special characters would be embedded raw. The `/vnc/status` default is `/vnc.html`, so in practice this is benign; only flagging for the proxy-with-auth-query case where an unencoded path could 404.
4. **Minor:** `data.get("vncPort")` inside the `resp.json()` block — if a proxy ever returned a non-object JSON, `resp.json()` could yield a non-dict and `.get` would raise `AttributeError`, which isn't in the caught tuple `(TypeError, ValueError, KeyError)`. A broader `except Exception` (as used on the `/vnc/status` branch) would be more uniform.

Well-structured and well-tested; nothing blocking.

payload.author: Enough1122

> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `gateway/config.py`, `plugins/platforms/discord/adapter.py`, new `tests/plugins/platforms/test_discord_dm_gate.py` + docs for PR #97771. Adding profile-scoped `discord.allow_dms` is well-motivated and the tests cover default-on, explicit off (bool and string forms), profile-over-env precedence, guild messages unaffected, and the real gateway loader path. Moving the `is_dm` computation ahead of the role/allowlist checks so the gate fires before any LLM admission is the right placement.

If `allow_dms: false` is intended to leave group-DM conversations reachable (some restricted profiles want group chats but not 1:1), this silently closes them too. Worth confirming the intended scope and documenting it — the docs only mention "Discord DMs".
2. **An explicit empty/`null` profile value falls through to "enabled".** `if "allow_dms" in extra:` → `raw = extra.get("allow_dms")` → if a user writes `allow_dms:` (YAML null) or an empty string, `raw is None or str(raw).strip() == ""` returns `True`. 3. **`config-first` inverts the documented env-wins rule for this key only.** The docs now say "Security ownership settings such as `discord.allow_dms` are config-first" — coherent and intentional, but a reader following the general "env var wins" contract may be surprised that `DISCORD_ALLOW_DMS=true` cannot re-open a profile that sets `allow_dms: false`. The doc note covers it; just flagging the asymmetry is intentional.

payload.title: fix(backup): bound incomplete snapshot retention

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `hermes_cli/backup.py` + tests for PR #97768. The change is a good correction to the #68805 behavior: instead of skipping pruning entirely whenever a snapshot is incomplete (which let stale secret-bearing partial snapshots accumulate unbounded), it always prunes to the keep window and adds one safety exception — preserve the newest complete snapshot as a recovery source. `preserve_latest_complete` scans manifests newest-first and retains the first snapshot with no `failed_dbs`/`oversized_skipped`. Tests cover both incomplete kinds (oversized/failed) and assert stale partials are removed while the complete recovery copy survives.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **The "preserve newest complete" scan ignores the keep window.** `retained = set(dirs[:keep])` then the scan adds the newest complete snapshot *regardless of age*. If the newest complete snapshot is already inside the kept window, the scan re-adds the same dir (harmless). But if a complete snapshot sits just outside the window, retention is effectively `keep + 1` even when the newer kept snapshots are also complete — slightly more aggressive retention than the intent ("when the retained window contains no complete snapshot"). Consider skipping the scan when any of `dirs[:keep]` is already complete, or documenting that `keep` is a floor.
2. **A "complete" snapshot may still be stale.** The preserved recovery copy can be arbitrarily old (state.db from weeks ago) — that is the stated intent (a recovery source), but the chosen newest complete may be much older than the user expects if failures persist. The warning message ("preserving latest complete recovery source") is accurate; just flagging the semantics for the message consumers.
3. **Corrupt manifest falls through silently.** A snapshot with an unreadable/corrupt `manifest.json` is skipped by the scan (never counted complete), so it can be pruned even if it contains the only good DB copy. Given manifests are written by the same tool this is unlikely, but a debug log on manifest parse failure would help if it ever happens.
4. **Minor:** the existing `test_oversized_db_suppresses_pruning` still passes (via the "skipping state.db" assertion), but its name and the removed "Skipping snapshot prune" message no longer reflect the new always-prune behavior — worth renaming/updating to assert the new "preserving latest complete" contract.

Solid fix with good test coverage; nothing blocking.

payload.title: fix(photon): persist inbound replay dedupe

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `plugins/platforms/photon/adapter.py` + tests for PR #97767. Making the at-least-once inbound dedupe durable is well-motivated (a sidecar/gateway restart previously forgot dispatched IDs), and the design is sound: the 48h/4000-ID window now lives under `HERMES_HOME/state`, is loaded with strict validation (finite timestamps, wall-clock rollback clamp, newest-bounded window), written atomically with mode `0600`, and persisted only after dispatch succeeds — so a failed dispatch is still retried after restart (covered by `test_failed_dispatch_is_retried_after_restart`). The profile-scoping and bound-eviction tests are solid.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **Full-file persist on every inbound message.** `_mark_seen_message()` calls `_persist_seen_messages()` on each new ID, which serializes and atomically rewrites up to 4,000 entries. On a high-throughput Photon channel this is one disk write per dispatched message. A debounce/throttle (e.g. flush at most every N seconds or N messages, plus on shutdown) would cut the write amplification without changing correctness — the in-memory dict already provides in-process replay protection.
2. **Crash between dispatch success and persist re-dispatches the replay.** That is the correct at-least-once trade-off (and the point of persisting after success), but it means the durability guarantee is "last successful dispatch may replay once" — worth stating in the docstring so operators don't expect exactly-once after a hard kill.
3. **File grows to 4,000 lines under `indent=0` + `separators`.** The state file is one JSON document regardless, so formatting is cosmetic only — not an issue, just noting it's the full bounded window on disk every flush.
4. **Minor:** `from hermes_constants import get_hermes_home` is a local import inside `__init__`; the other modules appear to import at top level. Local import is defensible here (keeps `adapter.py` import graph light), just inconsistent with the file's style.

The core fix is correct and well-tested; nothing blocking.

payload.author: sgtworkman
payload.title: fix(agent): preserve productive continuations and force overflow compaction

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `agent/conversation_loop.py` + tests for PR #97766. Two related changes: (1) replaces the fixed four-attempt continuation ceiling with a progress-based guard — stop only after three consecutive empty/duplicate fragments, fingerprinting each fragment by whitespace-normalized sha256 — and (2) adds `force=True` to `_compress_context` at the provider-proven overflow sites so automatic cooldown can't consume the retry budget without changing the transcript. Tests cover continuation beyond four fragments, duplicate-fragment cleanup, next-turn usability, and forced-overflow recovery.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **The fixed 4-attempt ceiling is replaced by a no-progress trigger with no absolute cap.** As long as each fragment is non-empty and *unique* (even trivially — e.g. a provider emitting `"a"`, `"ab"`, `"abc"`, … or churning out distinct tokens forever), `length_no_progress_retries` stays 0 and the loop keeps issuing continuation API calls until the outer per-turn budget (`max_iterations`) or an interrupt stops it. The set-based fingerprint does correctly catch alternation (A,B,A,B repeats an earlier fingerprint → no-progress → stop after 3), so the only unbounded case is endless *genuinely new* fragments. Consider an absolute continuation-attempt cap (even a generous one) on top of the no-progress guard to bound pathological burn-through of the iteration budget.

2. **Fingerprinting is content-exact, not progress-measured.** A fragment that only *slightly* advances (e.g. adds a few tokens to a stalled draft) counts as progress and resets the counter — reasonable, but it means the guard measures "new text appeared" rather than "meaningful progress". Acceptable proxy; just noting the semantics for anyone tuning the threshold.

3. **`force=True` at 4 sites.** The test covers one (output-cap overflow). The other three hunks sit in adjacent overflow/compression branches — worth a quick audit that each is genuinely *provider-proven* overflow (provider returned a concrete error) and not a heuristic-based compression, so forcing doesn't bypass a legitimate cooldown where the provider never actually rejected anything.

4. **Minor:** `length_continue_retries` appears to now be display-only (the `(attempt {length_continue_retries})` messages) while the gate uses the new counter; if it's no longer incremented anywhere, the display would pin at 0 — the diff doesn't show the increment line, so confirm it's either still incremented or the message is updated to the real attempt count.

The direction (progress-based instead of ceiling-based) fixes a real over-eager-stopping bug, and the overflow-force change is sensible; the main hardening ask is an absolute cap (observation 1). Nothing blocking.

payload.title: fix(bot-mode): avoid inherited stdin on Windows

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `tools/bot_mode_dm.py` + tests for PR #97758. Fixes the inherited-stdin failure on native Windows: query-file Bot Mode DM delivery (launched through Git Bash) could fail before the transport child starts because the child inherited Git Bash's invalid Windows stdin pseudo-handle. Both the initial attempt and the policy-gated retry path now pass `stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL`, while peer/stdin-file delivery keeps its real stream. The regression test asserts both attempts use DEVNULL, verifies returncode 0 and file unlink.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **`stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL` is applied unconditionally in the query-file branch, on all platforms.** On POSIX this is a harmless no-op improvement (a query-file child has no reason to read stdin); on Windows it's the fix. Applying it everywhere keeps the code simple and avoids a platform branch — correct call.

2. **Scope is right:** only the query-file `subprocess.run` calls changed; the `stdin_file=True` path that must preserve the real peer/stdin stream is untouched. The PR body's claim matches the diff.

3. **Test detail:** `fake_run` captures `kwargs["stdin"]` for both calls and asserts both are `subprocess.DEVNULL` — a meaningful behavioral assertion (not just "doesn't crash"). The two-step response (`HTTP 429` then success) exercises the retry path end-to-end.

4. **Minor:** `capture_output=True` still pipes stdout/stderr while stdin is DEVNULL — only the stdin side changed, which is the intended scope.

Clean, minimal fix with a targeted regression test. Nothing blocking.

payload.title: fix(config): recognize session reset policy fields

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `hermes_cli/config.py`, tests, and docs for PR #97757. Makes the gateway's existing fixed-shape `session_reset` fields recognizable to `hermes config set` via a new `_OPTIONAL_FIXED_CONFIG_SCHEMAS` map, without adding them to `DEFAULT_CONFIG` (preserving the opt-in runtime shape). Typo suggestions stay precise (`session_reset.notfy` → `session_reset.notify`), and the drift-guard test (`_OPTIONAL_FIXED_CONFIG_SCHEMAS["session_reset"]` == `SessionResetPolicy.__dataclass_fields__`) keeps CLI validation and gateway runtime fields in lockstep. Docs updated for the new `notify` toggle.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **The drift-guard test pins *exact* set equality.** Adding a legit field to either the dataclass or the schema without the other breaks CI — which is the intent (lockstep), but it means the schema must be updated in the same change as any gateway policy field. That's fine given the test exists; just noting the coupling is now explicit and load-bearing.

2. **Schema values are all `None` placeholders.** `_validate_config_key` uses the optional schema as the traversal node, so key *existence* is validated but there's no type/shape checking for these fields. That matches the "fixed-shape, runtime-defined" framing, but a user typo in the *value* (e.g. `notify: not-bool`) won't be caught here. Consistent with how the gateway treats it; only flagging the boundary.

3. **`DEFAULT_CONFIG.get(top, _OPTIONAL_FIXED_CONFIG_SCHEMAS.get(top))`** correctly gives precedence to an actual DEFAULT_CONFIG entry over the optional schema; for a top-level key absent from both, node stays None and existing handling applies. Verified no behavior change for non-`session_reset` keys.

4. **Minor:** `_OPTIONAL_FIXED_CONFIG_SCHEMAS` docstring explains the "why" well; the nested child values being None is a reasonable sentinel choice.

A focused, well-documented config-recognition fix with a strong drift guard. Nothing blocking.

payload.title: fix(weixin): preserve inbound preprocessing order per session

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `gateway/platforms/weixin.py` + tests for PR #97743. Preserves inbound preprocessing order per session: the poll loop returns an ordered batch, but each message became an independent task whose media download (before the base adapter's session guard) could reorder. The fix adds a per-session-key refcounted `asyncio.Lock` dict in `_process_message_safe`, serializing preprocessing within a session while keeping different sessions concurrent. Tests cover same-session ordering, cross-session concurrency, and failure-release.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **Per-session serialization also serializes media downloads.** Within one session, downloads that previously overlapped now run one-at-a-time (that's the point — order preservation), but a media-heavy chatty session gets serialized download latency. Correctness-over-throughput is the right call here; just noting the throughput cost is now explicit and per-session.

2. **The refcount pattern is more complex than a plain lock dict, and correctness depends on it.** The increment-before-`try`, decrement-in-`finally`, and `current[0] is lock` guard are all correct (a task holding a refcount prevents pop; the identity check defends against replacement). A short comment on the *waiter-race* (why refcounts rather than `dict.setdefault`) — the existing comment touches it but the invariant is subtle enough to warrant a few more words or a tiny helper, so future edits can't accidentally break it.

3. **`_inbound_order_key` recomputes the session key per message** by re-running `build_source` + `build_session_key` with the same params the generic guard uses. Good — it guarantees the two keys stay consistent by construction (both use the same shared helpers), so the lock scope exactly matches the base guard's session scope. No drift risk identified.

4. **Minor:** `test_failed_preprocessing_releases_session_queue` raises a `RuntimeError` from the fake, and the refcount cleanup in `finally` runs on both the exception and success paths — covered.

The fix is correct and well-tested for a real reordering bug. Nothing blocking.

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `agent/chat_completion_helpers.py`, contributor email file + `tests/run_agent/test_stale_connection_retry_97184.py` for PR #97741. Fixes a real retry gap: `httpx.ReadError("SSL: UNEXPECTED_EOF_WHILE_READING")` from a stale pooled connection was not classified as a transient connection error, so pre-delivery streams failed hard instead of retrying on a fresh pool. The fix adds `_httpx.ReadError` to `_is_conn_err` and `"unexpected_eof"` to both SSE phrase lists. Tests are thorough: baseline RemoteProtocolError retry, ReadError UNEXPECTED_EOF retry with a proven fresh client, wrapped `APIError` retry, and a non-transient no-retry sanity check.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **`_httpx.ReadError` is added wholesale, not just the EOF variant.** This classifies *all* read-level failures as transient, including ones that aren't stale-connection EOF (e.g., a malformed mid-stream response). Retries are bounded by `HERMES_STREAM_RETRIES` and use fresh pools, so risk is low — but the classification is coarser than the specific bug. If a distinct non-EOF ReadError family exists that shouldn't retry, the tuple could be tightened.

2. **Fresh-client proof via `id(m)`** (`created_ids[0] != created_ids[1]`) is slightly fragile (id reuse) but acceptable in tests; the call-count assertions are the load-bearing checks.

3. **`_make_agent` instantiates a real `AIAgent`** per test with `skip_context_files`/`skip_memory` — consistent with the project's E2E preference; fine.

4. **Minor:** the contributor email file (`contributors/emails/vaibhavdahiya28@gmail.com`) accompanies the fix — matches repo convention.

The fix addresses the reported failure mode precisely and is well-covered. Nothing blocking.

payload.title: feat(gateway): isolate workers and queue under resource pressure

payload.author: andrexibiza
payload.body:
Reviewed exact head `2ce15b344010ab37ba706194ddc2d3419a3c6025` against `main@9d9f44d63826b18503f44c754e48e1f4f83b3a6e`; the PR base is the current main object at review time. I read the resource-admission/cgroup/shutdown changes, the changed test surface, the existing evidence comments, #70716/#71023, and the live adjacent work in #57121, #97722/#97723, and #97825. There were no existing submitted reviews on this head, so this is not repeating an unchanged-head review.

There is a lot worth preserving here. The central `AgentAdmissionController`, FIFO queue, bounded queue notices, API/cron/background integration, `/background` drain/interrupt accounting, cgroup-v2 host-vs-service headroom witness, worker `MemoryHigh`/`MemoryMax`/`MemorySwapMax=0`, same-UID system-manager scope support, alert-only health guard, and structured shutdown evidence are all the right class of mechanisms. The PR also correctly separates the proved production restart initiator (the host health guard) from OOM claims instead of laundering correlation into causation. The exact-head author receipt of 279 passing tests plus the controlled 6-worker/3-slot crash-recovery stress is useful evidence.

I do see two P1 correctness/ownership blockers before this can close #70716.

### P1 — the default `auto` mode still falls back into the unsafe gateway cgroup on the exact production topology this PR measured

`hermes_cli/config_defaults.py` makes `terminal.worker_cgroup_mode` default to `"auto"`. In `tools/process_registry.py`, however, `_worker_scope_backend()` currently does:

```python
if mode in {"auto", "user", "required"} and _systemd_run_user_scope_available():
    return "user"
if mode in {"system", "required"} and _systemd_run_system_scope_available():
    return "system"
return None
```

So `auto` participates in the user-scope probe but **not** the system-scope fallback. That matters because the PR's own exact-host evidence says the `hermes-runtime` user scope is unavailable because there is no user bus, while the same-UID system scope passed.

On that host, the default configuration therefore resolves `auto -> None`. The background/PTTY `spawn_local()` paths then warn and spawn directly when mode is not `required`, leaving the worker in the gateway service cgroup. The foreground `LocalEnvironment._run_bash()` path likewise gets `backend is None` and does not wrap. In other words, a normal upgrade with the new defaults can still reproduce the core #70716 failure domain even though the PR has already proved that the system-scope escape hatch works on that machine.

That is exactly the distinction #70716 calls out: an opt-in guard is not closure if users remain unsafe after an ordinary upgrade unless they discover/configure the setting.

**Required fix:** make the default policy actually use the available safe backend — e.g. `auto` should try user scope first and then the same-UID system scope — or choose an equivalent default that guarantees isolation when the supported system backend is available. Please add the missing regression for `mode=auto`, user scope unavailable, system scope available => system scope selected, and exercise the foreground plus PTY/pipe spawn surfaces through that decision. `required` failing closed is good, but it does not make `auto` safe.

Until that is repaired, `Closes #70716` is too strong.

### P1 / merge-order — `/handoff` is still a second full-agent concurrency owner outside the new global admission controller

The new controller admits normal inbound turns, API runs, `/background`, and cron. It does not own the handoff watcher. The live #97722 / #97723 pair independently proves the other side of this shape: `_handoff_watcher` fire-and-forgets one **full agent turn plus delivery** per pending row; five pending rows reach five concurrent turns on main. #97723 currently fixes that with a separate closure-local semaphore of 3.

Those two mechanisms should not land independently as permanent peers. If #97739 is the reposit

payload.author: kzmx23
payload.title: feat(agent): master switch to disable the pre-agent auth fallback

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `gateway/run.py`, `hermes_cli/fallback_config.py` + tests for PR #97736. Adds a master kill-switch (`fallback.enabled`) with a backward-compatible default of True, wired into the gateway's pre-agent auth fallback (`_try_resolve_fallback_provider` returns None when disabled). The lenient scalar coercion, non-dict guard on the hot construction path, and `get_fallback_chain` non-dict hardening are all defensible; tests exercise the policy readers well.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **Scope vs. docstring mismatch.** `fallback_enabled`'s docstring claims manual mode means "NO automatic route change may occur at any layer — top-level chain, auxiliary fallback, summarizer to main, or pre-agent auth fallback", but this PR only gates the gateway's `_try_resolve_fallback_provider`. If the other layers (auxiliary fallback, summarizer→main, top-level chain consumers) don't consult `fallback_enabled`, then `fallback.enabled: false` won't actually disable them. Either wire those sites in this PR, or scope the docstring/feature claim down to "pre-agent auth fallback" so the docs don't over-promise.

2. **Unrecognized strings fail *open*.** `fallback.enabled: disabled`, `enabled`, `manual`, or any typo not in `_TRUE/_FALSE_TOKENS` silently defaults to the historical enabled=True — the opposite of what a kill-switch's operator intends. Given this is explicitly a safety switch, consider warning on unrecognized values (or treating them as False for a fail-closed posture), rather than silently keeping fallback on.

3. **`resolve_fallback_enabled_default` calls `load_config()` on every implicit agent construction** ("hot construction path"). If `load_config` is not cached, that's per-agent disk I/O on a hot path. Worth confirming it's cheap/cached, or memoizing the policy resolution.

4. **`bool(val)` for `int`/`float`** means `fallback.enabled: 0.0` → False and `2` → True; lenient but reasonable. Consistent with the documented coercion table.

The feature is well-tested and backward-compatible; the main follow-up is closing the gap between the docstring's "all layers" claim and the single site actually wired. Nothing blocking.

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `tools/transcription_tools.py` + `tools/tts_tool.py` for PR #97734. Surfaces plugin load failures instead of silently swallowing them (STT returns a named error envelope, TTS re-raises so the outer handler reports it), and routes plugin `max_text_length` through the resolver. The behavioral split is internally consistent with each module's contract: STT's dispatcher returns envelopes, TTS's dispatcher raises to the outer `try/except`. The `isinstance(limit, int) and not isinstance(limit, bool) and limit > 0` filtering is correctly defensive.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **The new TTS terminal-error branch changes prior fallthrough behavior.** The `elif provider not in BUILTIN_TTS_PROVIDERS:` branch now returns a hard error where the code previously fell through to the Edge TTS default. The comment asserts the only ways to reach it are "neither built-in, nor tts.providers command, nor registered plugin" — worth confirming the earlier `if`-chain really catches *every* legitimate provider type (custom command providers, any other resolution path), so no valid configuration silently becomes a hard failure. If any provider was previously resolved by a later branch, this would be a regression.

2. **`_resolve_max_text_length` calls `plugin_provider.list_models()`.** If that call raises (broken plugin) the resolver propagates rather than falling back — arguably correct (surface the broken plugin), but the surrounding code has no guard. Confirming the caller handles a raise here (or wrapping in the same "failed to load" treatment) would make the failure path explicit.

3. **STT envelope vs TTS re-raise asymmetry** is documented in each docstring and matches each module's convention — fine, just noting the two tools now fail differently by design.

4. **Minor:** `_ensure_plugins_discovered()` is called non-forced inside the resolver; an installed-but-not-yet-discovered plugin is the documented target case, so this is correct — only noting the timing dependency.

The change fixes a real observability gap (a broken plugin was indistinguishable from "not configured") and routes the TTS cap correctly. The main thing to double-check is observation 1's invariant. Nothing blocking.

Reviewed `agent/handoff.py`, `agent/insight_extraction.py`, `cli.py`, `hermes_cli/cli_commands_mixin.py`, `hermes_cli/commands.py` + tests for PR #97733. Adds durable session handoffs (extractive dependency-free default, LLM-summarized opt-in with strict-mode surfacing) plus durable-facts extraction that routes to an optional memory manager with zero extra LLM calls. The design is thoughtful: extractive fallback is genuinely dependency-free (keeps working during shutdown/compression failure), strict mode raises `HandoffLLMError` instead of silently downgrading a manual request, and test coverage is extensive (strict/non-strict, metadata append, index/symlink, excerpt truncation).

Non-blocking observations:

1. **Secrets hygiene in durable facts.** The module docstring explicitly delegates secret-protection to the memory store's write path and merely *asks* the model to omit secrets. `normalize_facts` is the last deterministic filter before long-term storage — a lightweight denylist for common credential patterns (`sk-…`, `ghp_…`, `Bearer …`) there would add defense-in-depth at the choke point. Worth considering given facts land in persistent memory.

2. **`_gather_git_context` runs `git log --oneline -20` / `git status` in `hermes_home`.** If the hermes home happens to be inside a git repo, up to 20 commit subjects get embedded into the handoff prompt and file. If the intent is project context, scoping to the actual project root (or truncating) would be tighter; otherwise worth a comment that home-directory git context is the intended scope.

3. **`_message_excerpt` keeps only head (1/4) + tail for long transcripts** (and max 80 msgs / 25k chars on the LLM path). Key decisions often sit in the omitted middle. An importance/salience-aware sample (or keeping the most tool-dense section) would materially improve handoff quality for long sessions; currently the middle is dropped on both paths.

4. **`_write_latest_pointer` symlink fallback:** on Windows without symlink privilege, `latest.md` becomes a *copy* of the target content and won't track later updates to the same target (stale pointer). Minor, but consider making the fallback re-write on each call (it does) and documenting the staleness.

5. **Cosmetic:** metadata format differs between paths — LLM path appends `platform: telegram` (lowercase, sorted), extractive path uses `Platform: telegram` (capitalized). Also, reusing `task="compression"` for the handoff call means the handoff inherits whatever provider/budget that task type resolves in `auxiliary_client`; `max_tokens=4000` for a full structured handoff may be tight — worth confirming that's intended.

6. **No E2E test** that `memory_manager.ingest_extracted_facts` actually fires on a real parsed facts block (the ingest is unit-tested via mocks). Given the rubric's E2E preference and that this is the one cross-module coupling, a small integration test would de-risk it.

A well-structured, well-tested feature with clean strict/fallback semantics. The points above are hardening suggestions, not blockers.

Reviewed `hermes_cli/subcommands/update.py` + `hermes_cli/update_cmd.py` for PR #97732. Adds `hermes update --merge-ref <ref>` to fetch one tag/ref from the fixed `upstream` remote and merge it into the current fork branch, bypassing the "Already up to date!" early-return (scoped correctly to the `origin/<branch>` comparison). Fail-closed behavior is well-handled: fetch failure, unresolved ref, and merge conflict each restore `pre_pull_sha` and exit non-zero before any install/dependency step runs. `--check`/`--merge-ref` mutual exclusion via an argparse group is the right way to avoid runtime validation.

3. **`FETCH_HEAD^{commit}` handling is correct** for annotated tags, and `--no-edit` is a sound non-interactivity assumption (consistent with the rest of the updater). The manual-recovery message prints the right pre-pull SHA on restore failure.

payload.author: andrexibiza
payload.body:
Reviewed exact head `05b9932aeaec6d229b703aec9158317b5ac7426a` against base `10e93c6ab958c7ec61cfc4416f4d4459e72ca8a7` and current `main@1d8946b40b9333a7fda81be890be31771a312d4f`.

The underlying bug is real, and this head does close the **pristine** no-callback fail-open: the new `approval_unavailable` branch prevents a destructive action from reaching the backend when `_approval_callback` is actually `None`, and the isolation regression now pins that state. That is useful work to preserve.

I cannot clear this head yet because two authority boundaries are still wrong.

## P1 — `cb is None` is not equivalent to “no approval surface exists”

The new branch in `tools/computer_use/tool.py::_request_approval()` says:

> `No prompt surface is wired (headless, gateway, messaging runs).`

but the predicate is only `cb = _approval_callback; if cb is None`. `_approval_callback` is the **CLI-local** callback. Current `tools.approval` already owns the wider approval contexts through `request_tool_approval()` / `_run_approval_gate`: gateway sessions can do the normal notification/button round-trip, cron honors `approvals.cron_mode`, single-query honors `approvals.single_query_mode`, and a genuinely non-interactive/no-human context fails closed.

So this head trades the fail-open for an over-broad hard denial:

- a Discord/Telegram/Slack-style gateway user with a reachable approval responder gets `approval_unavailable` instead of the repository's normal approval round-trip;
- `approvals.cron_mode: approve` is ignored for `computer_use`;
- `approvals.single_query_mode: approve` is ignored for `computer_use`.

This is already the key distinction documented on #87724 by jackulau, implemented in closed #87782, and then adopted into QDung210's still-open #87764. Those are not unrelated duplicates: they establish the existing product-policy path this patch currently bypasses.

**Required fix:** when there is no local callback, enter the shared approval authority with the existing `(action, delivery_mode)` scope, and fail closed only when that authority has neither an explicit unattended grant nor a reachable human. Preserve the prior contributors' work rather than re-inventing the policy locally.

There is one merge-order caveat: do not blindly copy #87764's current bridge. Open #61064 tracks the shared-gate ordering defect where a prior `Always` approval can override unattended `cron_mode: deny`. `computer_use` should not introduce a new permanent grant path that widens its existing session-owned `_always_allow` / `_session_auto_approve` semantics. Either compose the shared-gate ordering fix first, or make the bridge explicitly non-permanent/session-owned and add prior-grant → cron-deny + single-query-deny regressions.

## P1 — callback ownership is still process-global, so the headless class is not actually closed

At this head `_approval_callback` is still a module-global value. That means `cb is None` is not a session-owned fact. In a process serving concurrent sessions:

1. session A installs an interactive callback;
2. session B is headless and has no responder of its own;
3. session B observes A's process-global callback, skips this new fail-closed branch entirely, and can route its mutation through A's responder.

That is the other side of the same authority shape: absence/presence must be bound to the owning execution context, not ambient process state. Open #81668 (jjjinz) already isolates this callback with a `ContextVar` and includes a concurrent two-session regression. It is complementary ownership work, not superseded by this PR.

**Required fix:** compose/rebase the session-owned callback isolation (or carry an explicit session-owned approval capability into `handle_computer_use`) and add a concurrency regression where one context has a callback and a second callback-free context performs a destructive action. The second context must never invoke the first context's responder and must enter the shared headless approval path / fai

payload.author: pixelatedhacker
payload.body:
Thanks for the exact-head review — both P1s are fair, and this head now addresses them.

**P1 #1 (cb is None ≠ no approval surface):** agreed. The no-callback branch no longer hard-denies; it escalates through the repository's normal gate via `tools.approval.request_tool_approval()`, so gateway sessions get the standard approval round-trip, cron honors `approvals.cron_mode`, single-query honors `approvals.single_query_mode`, and a context with no possible responder still fails closed (`code: approval_unavailable`). Only the pristine case (`_approval_callback` absent, no responder anywhere) keeps the immediate denial.

**Merge-order caveat:** I did not adopt a permanent-grant bridge. The `rule_key` passed to the gate embeds the *approval* session key (`computer_use:<session_key>:<cu_session_id>:<action>:<delivery>`), so an `[a]lways` answered interactively is scoped to that approval session by construction and cannot short-circuit an unattended context that reuses the same computer_use `session_id`. This sidesteps the shared-gate ordering defect in #61064 rather than widening it; `computer_use`'s own `_always_allow` / `_session_auto_approve` semantics are unchanged. Regressions added: prior interactive grant → cron run still denied (`cron_mode` default deny), and prior grant → single-query run still denied.

**P1 #2 (process-global callback):** `set_approval_callback` now stores the callback in a `ContextVar` and returns a token for a new `reset_approval_callback()` (same shape as #81668 — this composes that ownership fix inline; happy to rebase onto #81668 if it lands first, the two diffs touch the same seams). The concurrency regression you asked for is in: a callback-free context performing a destructive action while another context's responder is installed must never invoke that responder — it enters the shared headless approval path and fails closed.

**Base/CI:** rebased onto current `main` (1d8946b40b93...). Hosted CI still shows `action_required` on my side — I can't self-approve those runs, so maintainer approval is what's left for the exact-head receipt.

Reviewed `gateway/run.py` + tests for PR #97723. Adds `_HANDOFF_MAX_CONCURRENT = 3` with a per-watcher `asyncio.Semaphore` so a post-outage backlog of N pending handoff rows cannot open N parallel full agent turns. The design is well-chosen: only the agent-turn portion of the dispatch holds a slot, while `complete_handoff` terminal-state bookkeeping runs outside the semaphore, so completion never waits on the cap. payload.title: fix(skills): keep the skill and snapshots when a batch rollback restore fails

payload.author: lEWFkRAD
payload.body:
**Blocking review (formal CHANGES_REQUESTED is unavailable to this account):** the rollback destination is still not collision-safe.

1. **P1 - unrelated data can be deleted.** `aside = post_dir.with_name(post_dir.name + '.rollback-broken')` is a predictable sibling name, and `.rollback-broken` is permitted by the existing skill/category name grammar. `shutil.rmtree(aside, ignore_errors=True)` therefore deletes a legitimate pre-existing sibling skill/category before the rollback starts. Please allocate an exclusive temporary path (for example with `tempfile` under a private rollback root), never a user-addressable skill name, and fail closed if an exclusive move cannot be established.

2. **Cleanup failure is reported as success.** After a successful `copytree`, `shutil.rmtree(aside, ignore_errors=True)` can silently leave the half-applied directory behind. Because that sibling name is itself discoverable as a valid skill name, this can leave a stale duplicate active while `_rollback()` reports success and the `finally` removes the recovery snapshot. Cleanup failure must be surfaced and the snapshot retained until the aside copy is positively removed (or moved to a non-discoverable private location).

3. **The regression test does not prove the recovery invariant.** It only asserts that the half-applied live skill survives. It never asserts that the retained snapshot exists, is the exact pre-batch tree/content, and is uniquely attributable to this operation; the failed-rollback path also leaks its `skill_batch_*` temp tree. Please bind the temp location to the test, assert the exact original snapshot is retained (without scanning unrelated global temp directories), and clean it up explicitly.

These are blocking because the proposed recovery path can itself erase unrelated valid user data and can falsely report a complete rollback.

payload.author: andrexibiza
payload.body:
Reviewed exact head `eea34e63d0c4b1505cb32b4e287fb9b3f384f5bd` against its recorded base `10e93c6ab958c7ec61cfc4416f4d4459e72ca8a7` and live `main@aff5125f8edf5095aef5d3d79bbbb101c95b9413` (14 commits past that base). I read the eight-file diff, the full hosted-room store and `groups.*` surface, the focused room/RPC/install-identity tests, the predecessor/supersession history, the stacked runner, the live issue contracts, and the exact-head workflow state. There were no comments or reviews on #97712 when I started.

A lot of the hard authority work from closed-unmerged predecessor #95314 survived the recut correctly: owner identity is server-derived rather than client-asserted; first-install identity publication/repair is cross-process serialized; legacy adoption advances the epoch and emits a real `authority.claimed` lineage receipt; schema upgrades are transactional; event sequence allocation and authority claims are fenced; client ingress cannot forge member/gateway events; and `driver: false` remains an honest boundary. The new store also stays below the godfile ceiling at 1,274 lines rather than putting the room implementation into `tui_gateway/server.py`. That is substantial, careful work. 🚀

I do have one P1 blocker introduced by the new `fix(bot-mode): bound hosted Group Chat history` commit: **the retention policy deletes the identity tombstone, so a disbanded immutable `room_id` can become a different room later (ABA).**

`#95163` is explicit that the authoritative tables are keyed by the **immutable `roomId` “honoring final id-tombstones.”** This PR encodes the same contract in `disband_room()` (“Permanently tombstone a room id”), and `tests/gateway/test_hosted_rooms.py::test_disband_is_idempotent_and_room_id_cannot_be_reused` correctly proves reuse is rejected while the tombstone exists.

But the new `_prune_disbanded_rooms_locked()` in `gateway/hosted_rooms.py` selects disbanded rooms after the 90-day window, after the retained-tombstone count exceeds `MAX_DISBANDED_ROOM_TOMBSTONES`, or under gateway byte pressure, then executes both:

```py
DELETE FROM hosted_room_events WHERE room_id IN (...)
DELETE FROM hosted_rooms WHERE room_id IN (...)
```

After that second delete, `create_room()` finds no existing row and takes the fresh-room INSERT path for the same `room_id`. The new `test_room_listing_is_paged_and_old_tombstones_are_pruned` actually proves the first half of this sequence by making `room-0` disappear once the tombstone bound is crossed; it never exercises the other side of the shape by attempting to create `room-0` again.

That turns bounded history retention into identity reuse. A stale client, replay cursor, future task/cancellation record, or cross-gateway envelope carrying the old room coordinate can now alias a different logical Group Chat after pruning. This is exactly the failure the authority layer is otherwise designed to prevent: a coordinate that once named terminal generation A becomes valid again for generation B with no proof object distinguishing them. It also breaks the PR-body claim that writes after disband are rejected as a durable property; they are rejected only until retention pressure erases the evidence.

**Required repair:** separate payload/history retention from identity retirement. It is fine to bound or purge old event payloads, but keep a compact permanent retired-ID record (in `hosted_rooms` or a dedicated retired-room table) that `create_room()` consults forever, so a final room identity never returns to the fresh namespace. If disband replay itself is retention-bounded, make the expired-history state typed/explicit; do not turn “history no longer retained” into “this identity never existed.” An alternative is a server-issued globally unique room identity plus a durable non-reuse guarantee, but client-selected IDs cannot be made reusable under the present contract.

payload.author: kshitijk4poor
payload.body:
Status: converting to draft — @cervantesh's review on #97158 contains one blocker this salvage fixes and one it does not.

**Fixed here:** the cleanup regression (blocker 2). `affinity_token` is initialized alongside `token`, and the 4 previously-red cross-process lease tests are green on this branch (12/12).

**Verified still present (blocker 1):** the `/new` lifetime violation. Reproduced on this exact head with the resolver + a real `SessionDB`:

```python
db.create_session('sess-A', source='telegram')
a = agent(session_id='sess-A', _gateway_session_key=K)
db.create_session('sess-B', source='telegram')   # what /new produces — same chat key K
b = agent(session_id='sess-B', _gateway_session_key=K)
resolve_prompt_cache_scope(a)  # gwk_e545a9eb80a9283345539b21
resolve_prompt_cache_scope(b)  # gwk_e545a9eb80a9283345539b21  ← does NOT rotate
```

`gateway/session.py::reset_session()` mints a fresh physical id but keeps the chat key, so declared-key precedence maps pre- and post-`/new` conversations onto one affinity scope — violating the #79017/#86733 contract (continuity across compression rotation, reset on `/new`/`/branch`), and doing so for every native messaging gateway, not just per-response hosts.

**What a correct carrier needs** (matching the review's criteria): stable across per-response physical ids within one logical conversation, rotating on `/new`. The chat key alone cannot provide that — it needs a per-conversation epoch mixed in (e.g. a value minted at `reset_session()`/conversation creation and carried alongside the key), which is a design change to the declaration contract, not a follow-up commit.

Holding this salvage as draft until the lifecycle question is settled on #97158. The `affinity_token` fix commit here remains valid for whichever revision lands.

payload.author: kshitijk4poor
payload.title: fix(vertex): pick up rotated service-account files — signature-keyed creds cache

payload.author: unsupportedpastels
payload.body:
## Security review: one medium-severity finding

### Medium — credential rotation can still reuse the old credentials object

**`agent/vertex_adapter.py:128-130`**

The cache fingerprint uses only:

```text
(path, mtime_ns, size)
```

Those attributes do not uniquely identify the credential contents. An atomic replacement can contain different credentials while retaining the previous file’s size and modification time. This occurs with metadata-preserving deployment/configuration tools and can also be deliberately produced.

I reproduced this against PR head `1e0ad60a8134a5fb64663e4d81a824a82f704410`:

```text
inode_changed=True
content_changed=True
cache_keys_equal=True
credentials_reloaded=False
```

In that case, Hermes continues using the cached private key and token despite the service-account file having been replaced. That undercuts the PR’s security objective: reliably picking up credential rotation without restarting.

The new rotation test does not cover this because it changes the file size and explicitly advances its mtime.

**Suggested remediation:** fingerprint the actual bytes, ideally reading the small JSON file once and constructing credentials from that same snapshot. This also avoids a stat/read TOCTOU window. A weaker but cheaper improvement would include device, inode, and change time, which catches ordinary atomic replacements but is not as definitive as a content digest. Add a regression test replacing the file with different, equal-length content while preserving `mtime_ns`.

### Other observations

- The ADC-to-service-account retry correction is sound and tested.
- Superseded cache entries are bounded by path.
- No new injection, path traversal, secret disclosure, or dependency exposure found in the diff.
- Focused tests: **9 passed**.
- Ruff: **passed**.
- Semgrep auto rules: **no findings**.
- GitHub’s supply-chain, OSV, Windows/macOS, and lint checks passed; the full Python test job and Nix check were still running when reviewed.

**Verdict:** narrow and directionally correct, but the stated credential-rotation guarantee remains incomplete due to the metadata-signature collision. No review or comment was posted to GitHub.

payload.author: kshitijk4poor
payload.body:
**Review-gate result (folded as the follow-up commit):**

The /simplify-code reviewer caught a real regression in my first commit: the ADC-failure → SA-retry fallback still compared `cache_key == "__adc__"` (string) after the keying change made every key a tuple — always-False, retry silently dead, and no existing test covered that path so 8/8 green didn't catch it.

Folded: the guard now tests the actual condition (`not resolved_path`) instead of a key-shape literal, so it can't rot again; plus a regression test driving the full ADC-fails → SA-file-appears → retry-succeeds path. Verified three ways: the test fails with the broken string comparison re-introduced, passes on main (whose string keys made the old comparison work — confirming this was a would-be regression my PR introduced and now closes), and 9/9 on the branch. Mutation check re-run on the final stack: main prod → 3 fail; restored → 9/9 green.

payload.author: kshitijk4poor
payload.body:
@unsupportedpastels Verified and fixed — thank you, this was a real hole in the PR's core guarantee.

**Reproduced your collision first** (equal-length content, `os.utime` restore, `os.replace`): `inode_changed=True content_changed=True cache_keys_equal=True` — exactly your result. The stat idiom I borrowed is right for the config caches it came from (guards a *parse*; a metadata-identical miss is harmless) and wrong for this one (guards an *identity*).

**Folded as `9ce700f`, your suggested remediation in full (the strong form):**
- Key is now `(path, sha256(content))` via a new `_read_sa_file()` that returns both the bytes and the key from ONE read; on a miss, credentials are built from that same snapshot via `from_service_account_info` — so the stat→read TOCTOU you noted is closed too (key and credentials can never describe different bytes).
- Read failure degrades to the bare-path key + the SDK's own file read — byte-for-byte the pre-signature behavior.
- Cost: one read+sha256 of ~2KB JSON per cache probe, noise next to the token mint the cache avoids.

**Your requested regression test is in:** equal-length replacement with `mtime_ns` preserved and atomic `os.replace` → asserts new cache key + new Credentials object. Mutation-checked: it FAILS against the stat-keyed commit (reproducing your `cache_keys_equal=True`) and against origin/main; 10/10 green on the branch.

Re-armed auto-merge (rebase).

- **/simplify-code on the final stack:** one finding, folded as the last commit — after the content-digest rework, `_creds_cache_key()` had become a wrapper with zero production callers, kept alive only by its own tests. ## Native Win11 verify (monerostar)

Host: Windows 11 (build 26200), Python 3.11.15, pytest 9.1.1. `shutil.which("bash")` on this box is the Hermes-bundled Git Bash:

`C:\Users\Admin\AppData\Local\hermes\git\usr\bin\bash.EXE`

`uname -s` → `MINGW64_NT-10.0-26200`

### Before (current `main` `_bash_path`)

`tests/test_install_sh_uv_lock_config.py::test_locked_sync_helper_sanitizes_only_its_subprocess` fails with **exit 127**:

```
AssertionError: /usr/bin/bash: /mnt/c/Users/Admin/AppData/Local/Temp/pytest-of-Admin/.../harness.sh: No such file or directory
assert 127 == 0
```

Git Bash does not mount the Windows drive at `/mnt/c`. That path is WSL-only. Matches the PR description.

### After this PR

Same test: **1 passed** in 0.45s.

`test_installers_keep_bootstrap_isolation_but_restore_project_config_for_lock`: **1 passed**.

The `uname` probe is the right split: MINGW/MSYS/CYGWIN keep `path.as_posix()` (`C:/...`); Linux uname keeps `/mnt/<drive>/...` for WSL. POSIX early-return unchanged.

Fixes #97698 on a real Git Bash Windows developer machine. No production code in the diff.

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `hermes_cli/gateway.py` + tests for PR #97699. Adds a legacy-name fallback (`com.hermes.gateway` → `ai.hermes.gateway`) to both `get_launchd_plist_path()` and `get_launchd_label()`, so upgraded machines whose launchd service kept the pre-rename label are found by status/start/stop. The four tests cover legacy-only, canonical-wins, no-plist, and profiled cases — solid coverage of the branch matrix.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **Legacy-resolution logic is duplicated across the two functions** with slightly different shapes: `get_launchd_plist_path` checks `not path.exists() and legacy.exists()`, while `get_launchd_label` checks `legacy_plist.exists() and not canonical_plist.exists()`. Functionally equivalent, but each independently re-derives the same "which service is active" decision, so they can drift (or disagree transiently if a plist is created between the two calls). A shared helper would keep them provably in lockstep.

2. **`launchd_gateway_labels_for_install()` is unchanged.** If any operation enumerates labels via that function (e.g., a stop-all/status-across-labels path), the legacy service may still be missed there. Worth confirming whether any consumer relies on the label set from that function and, if so, whether it should also include the legacy name.

3. **`get_launchd_plist_path()` is no longer a pure path function** — it now performs filesystem existence checks. For callers that write a fresh plist on first install, this is a behavior change (though on a fresh machine neither plist exists, so it returns canonical). Intentional and documented, just flagging the semantic shift.

The fix matches the described root cause (label + plist lookup both missed the legacy name) and the tests verify it. Nothing blocking.

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `agent/agent_runtime_helpers.py` + tests for PR #97697. Elevates the dropped-positional-orphan log from DEBUG to WARNING and adds a `caplog` regression. The change is exactly as scoped: the stub log stays at DEBUG (a stub repairs an unanswered call and destroys nothing), while a dropped real result — which the model explicitly asked for — is now visible in `errors.log`. The reasoning is sound and the diff is minimal.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **WARNING may be noisy on strict providers.** For providers where orphaned results are a routine repair (the #97203 pairing walk), every affected turn now emits a WARNING into `errors.log`. That's the intent, but if the rate turns out high, a rate-limited/aggregated counter might keep the signal without log spam. Purely a tuning question.

2. **`_ra()` logger vs `caplog` filter.** The test filters `caplog.at_level(logging.WARNING, logger="run_agent")` but the assertion itself just scans records for `levelno == WARNING`. If `_ra().logger`'s name isn't exactly `run_agent`, the level filter silently doesn't apply (records are still captured globally), so the test still passes — the logger-name assumption isn't actually pinned. Consider asserting the record's `name` to lock the intended logger.

3. **Minor:** the docstring/comment block added before the call is clear and matches house style; nothing to change.

The behavior change is one line plus a comment and a test — low-risk and addresses a real observability gap. Nothing blocking.

payload.author: Adolanium
payload.title: fix(config): register file_tools.hosted_ocr, opt-in keyless hosted OCR

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `tools/read_extract.py`, `hermes_cli/config_defaults.py`, `cli-config.yaml.example` + tests for PR #97688. Commit 1 (registering `file_tools.hosted_ocr` in `DEFAULT_CONFIG` + the example config) fixes a real gap from #97195 — an unregistered key silently ignored by the deep-merge/setup. Commit 2's resolution logic (false = off, true = keyless opt-in, null/default = key-gated) is coherent, well-documented, and the refactor of `hosted_ocr_available()` to delegate to `_hosted_ocr_config()` removes genuine duplication. Tests cover the gate states and the keyless retry path (`ocr='hosted'` with no `api_key`).

Non-blocking observations:

1. **`is True` / `is False` identity checks ignore non-bool values.** `setting is True` / `setting is False` — a YAML value that parses to something else (e.g. a quoted `"true"` string, `1`, `yes`) would be silently treated as "null/auto" and key-gated. The prior code used the same `is False` convention so this is consistent, but `== True`/`== False` (or a small normalization) would be more forgiving of config typos.

2. **Schema wording vs. keyless mode.** `hosted_ocr_available()` now returns True for `hosted_ocr: true` with no key, which drives the `read_file` schema line ("PDF (scanned or text)"). Worth confirming the schema text is mode-agnostic and doesn't tell a keyless opt-in user they must set `FIRECRAWL_API_KEY` (the NEEDS-OCR warning text is referenced as the fallback curriculum, but the schema line is what the model reads at call-build time).

3. **Keyless egress is an upload with no account/credential.** With `hosted_ocr: true` and no key, scanned PDFs go to firecrawl.dev's free tier unauthenticated — rate limits and any data-retention caveats of the keyless tier are now the user's exposure. The config comment documents this ("sends the document to Firecrawl's Parse endpoint"), which is the right consent framing; just flagging it so the trade-off is consciously shipped.

4. **Minor:** the `test_runtime_keyless_route_with_opt_in` patch chains use inline-whitespace line breaks (e.g. `patch.object(rx, "_hosted_ocr_config",` newline `return_value=...`) that read awkwardly; cosmetic only.

Both commits are internally consistent and the registration fix stands alone as claimed; nothing blocking.

payload.author: Adolanium
payload.body:
Thanks for the review. Went through all four points:

1. Valid, fixed in e4c7a2f88 (folded into the feature commit so it is correct as a unit). Quoted values from hand-edited YAML now go through a tri-state coercion using the same token table as `hermes config set` (true/1/yes/on, false/0/no/off). The expensive direction was a quoted `'false'` silently failing to disable the outbound call when a key is set. Anything unrecognized still reads as auto, matching the repo's existing `Optional[bool]` coercers (same shape as `tools/video_generation_tool.py`). New test covers quoted true/false, `yes`, quoted `1`, and unrecognized values (string, int, list).

2. Verified moot: the schema line is exactly one dynamic word, `PDF (text layer)` becomes `PDF (scanned or text)`. Nothing in the schema text mentions `FIRECRAWL_API_KEY` or any route, for either mode.

3. Agreed on the framing, no code change. The default (null) stays key-gated and the config comment states the upload in plain words, so keyless only happens for a user who wrote `true` themselves.

4. Left as-is: the wide whitespace runs in the test file match the style of the surrounding `#97195` tests, so keeping them consistent reads better than reflowing just the new lines.

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `apps/desktop/src/plugins/hermes-bots/plugin.tsx` + tests for PR #97683. The root cause is clearly identified and the fix is minimal: `message_agent` targets were annotated from `botHandle()`'s source-qualified UI alias (`default-vera`), which neither `resolve_remote_target()` (canonical handle/profile ± `@connection-id`) nor the local path accepts. Switching the remote branch to `${bot.name}@${bot.connectionId}` and adding a relay test for the `profile@connection` form is the right, narrow fix. The test updates accurately pin the new canonical form and guard against the alias leaking back in.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **The local branch still passes through `botHandle(bot.name)`.** For a remote bot the alias is now avoided, but a non-remote (local) bot still gets `target = botHandle(bot.name)`. If `botHandle()` ever returns the source-qualified UI alias for a local row too (the comment describes it as preferring that alias generally), the local `message_agent` target would hit the same "not resolvable" bug the PR fixes for remote bots. A test covering the local (no `remoteSource`) path — asserting the target is the bare canonical profile name — would make the invariant explicit. (If `botHandle` is known to return the canonical name for local rows, a brief comment would suffice.)

payload.author: kshitijk4poor
payload.title: fix(teams): authenticate Bot Framework connector attachment downloads (pasted images 401)

payload.author: Enough1122
payload.body:
> AI code review — automated review for reference; please use your judgment.

Reviewed `plugins/platforms/teams/adapter.py` + tests for PR #97677. The fix is well-targeted: pasted/inline images arrive on Bot Framework connector hosts that need the bot's own bearer token, and the change routes them through an authenticated fetch while leaving SharePoint `downloadUrl` file uploads untouched. The dot-anchored `_is_botframework_attachment_host` predicate is correct (rejects `evil-trafficmanager.net` / `notbotframework.com`, verified by tests), the token is cached with a 5-minute pre-expiry buffer, and token-acquisition failure degrades to a warned unauthenticated fetch rather than crashing. Test coverage is strong, including the attacker-lookalike case and the invalid-bytes warning regression guard.

Non-blocking observations:

1. **Bearer token and cross-host redirects.** The `Authorization` header is attached to the original request and the client follows redirects (`follow_redirects=True`) with `_ssrf_redirect_guard` on the response event. httpx strips `Authorization` on cross-host redirects by default, and the guard validates redirect targets, so the token shouldn't leak — but this is the one token-exfiltration boundary in the change. Worth confirming (ideally with a test) that a BF-host URL that 302s to an attacker host is both blocked by `_ssrf_redirect_guard` and never carries the `Authorization` header on the cross-host request, so the safety doesn't silently depend on httpx internals.

2. **Gov/sovereign cloud hosts are not covered.** The adapter already whitelists government endpoints (`smba.infra.gov.teams.microsoft.us` in `_ALLOWED_TEAMS_SERVICE_HOSTS`), but `_is_botframework_attachment_host` only matches `*.trafficmanager.net` / `*.botframework.com`, and the token endpoint is hardcoded to `login.microsoftonline.com`. Pasted images in gov/sovereign-cloud tenants will therefore still 401 (no token attached), and even if they were detected, the token request would go to the wrong authority (`login.microsoftonline.us` for GCC High/DoD). If gov-cloud support is in scope for Teams, the host predicate and token authority need to be tiered; if it's explicitly out of scope, a comment documenting that would prevent future confusion.

3. **No retry on transient token-endpoint failure.** `_get_botframework_token` performs one POST with a 15s timeout; a transient network blip fails the whole attachment with a warning and an unauthenticated fetch that will 401 anyway. A single bounded retry (or a short-lived negative cache) would make pasted images more resilient without much complexity. Minor.

4. **Minor:** `_get_botframework_token` mutates `self._bf_token_cache` without a lock — fine for the adapter's serialized loop, but worth a note if the adapter ever processes messages concurrently. Also, `_fetch_attachment_bytes` does a fresh `login.microsoftonline.com` round-trip per adapter instance on cold cache; acceptable.

The change matches its stated symptom and is well tested; nothing blocking.
